weeks.title: Getting to Know Someone
weeks.theme: Look at a person not only for what he says, but also for the fruit he bears over the long run.
group: Read Matt 7:16–20. By what does Jesus say we can recognize a person? Why is this standard more reliable than “feelings”?
For someone you are getting to know, or someone you once liked, what “fruit” in his life have you already seen?
What method do you want to use this week to get to know someone more honestly and more lovingly? Ask your group members to pray for you.
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, ask a mature brother or sister to spend three minutes telling you: “What fruit do you see in my life?” Then spend three more minutes taking turns praying for each other, asking God to make you both bear good fruit.
weeks.weekend: This weekend arrange “getting to know someone in a group”: invite someone you want to know better to eat or serve with other friends. Observe how he treats the server, how he treats those weaker than himself, and how he handles a difference of opinion. When you get home, write down only your observations, draw no conclusions, and share them with a trusted friend.

lessons.title: By Their Fruits
lessons.hear:
Xiaojie met a brother who was a gifted speaker. His prayers on stage were moving, and his posts on Facebook were full of love. But Xiaojie occasionally noticed that he was rude to restaurant servers and often did not keep his promises to friends. She talked herself into it: he’s just under a lot of stress.

Jesus said, “By their fruits you will know them.” (Matt 7:16) Their fruit is their long-term behavior, attitudes, and relationships, not one or two performances, and not how well they speak.

This does not mean we should nitpick people, or judge everyone by a single standard. It means we should open our eyes and look with God’s standard: How does he treat the weak? Is he honest? Does he take responsibility? What is he like when people aren’t watching? Fruit takes time, and it takes observation. We must also be willing to be measured by this same standard ourselves.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his fruit is love, mercy, and truth, consistent and lasting. The Bible is my standard: we know people by their fruits, and we know ourselves too. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he lets me see the truth and gives me gentleness. Those who live for self judge by feelings; those who live in selflessness let the Holy Spirit and the Bible be the standard of judgment.
think: According to Matt 7:16, by what are we to recognize a person?
Have I ever overlooked someone’s fruit because of his eloquence, looks, or my feelings?
How would other people see my own fruit today?
lessons.speak: Lord, open my eyes, so that I am not deceived by eloquence and feelings, and can see the real fruit of a person’s life. Examine my own life too, and let me bear fruit that pleases you. Holy Spirit, give me wisdom, and give me a gentle heart. Amen.
lessons.do: Today write down three specific behaviors you have already seen in someone you know, in the areas of “honesty, responsibility, and attitude toward the weak.” Draw no conclusions; write only facts.
lessons.quick: To know a person, look at the long-term fruit, not only at what he says.
text: By their fruits you will know them. Do you gather grapes from thorns or figs from thistles?
Even so, every good tree produces good fruit, but the corrupt tree produces evil fruit.
A good tree can’t produce evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree produce good fruit.
Every tree that doesn’t grow good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.
Therefore by their fruits you will know them.

lessons.title: The Good Person Out of the Good Treasure of His Heart
lessons.hear:
Zhe easily lost his temper in front of friends, and afterward he always said, “I just spoke too quickly. My heart isn’t like that.” But his girlfriend gradually noticed that his words often carried contempt.

Jesus said, “The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings out that which is good, and the evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings out that which is evil, for out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks.” (Luke 6:45) A person’s words and actions flow out of the heart. An occasional slip of the tongue happens to everyone, but a long-term attitude deserves to be taken seriously.

This saying is also spoken to ourselves. We should not only look at other people’s hearts, but also let God examine ours. Ask God to make what is stored in my heart his love, and not my own pride, control, and insecurity. When the heart is changed, words and actions will be changed.

Be careful not to treat “he has a heart to change” as “he has already changed.” Change takes time, and it takes action.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his heart was full of love, so everything that came out of him was life. The Bible is my standard: the good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings out what is good. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he renews my heart, so that I bear new fruit. Those who live for self only polish their words and actions; those who live in selflessness let God renew the heart.
think: According to Luke 6:45, where do a person’s words and actions come from?
What is stored most often in my heart: love, resentment, or insecurity?
What can I ask God for today so that my heart is renewed?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, examine my heart, and bring pride, resentment, and control into the light. Fill me with your love, so that what is stored in my heart is good and what comes out is life. Help me also to be patient with other people’s change, without easily believing a single sentence. Amen.
lessons.do: Today find a quiet time and say to God: “Please examine my heart.” Then write down three emotions or thoughts you notice, without criticizing, just being honest.
lessons.quick: When the heart is changed, words and actions will be changed, and change takes time and action.
text: For each tree is known by its own fruit. For people don’t gather figs from thorns, nor do they gather grapes from a bramble bush.

The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings out that which is good, and the evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings out that which is evil, for out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks.

lessons.title: Counsel in the Heart of Man
lessons.hear:
Hao wanted to get to know a certain brother better but didn’t know how to start. He always asked, “How have you been?” and the other always answered, “Fine.” After two months, they were still at the surface.

Proverbs says, “Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water,” but a man of understanding will draw it out. (Prov 20:5) A person’s inner life is like deep water, and it takes someone with wisdom and patience to draw it up. This means that getting to know a person is not an interrogation, and it is not seeing through him all at once. It is entering slowly through good questions and patient listening.

You can ask, “What has moved you most about God lately?” or “What is something you have learned a lesson from?” Remember also that deep water should not be dragged up by force. If the other person does not want to share, respect that; if he keeps avoiding important questions, you also don’t need to force yourself to ignore it.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he entered people’s hearts with questions, as with the Samaritan woman. The Bible is my standard: a man of understanding draws out the deep water. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives me wisdom to ask and patience to listen. Those who live for self are quick to reach conclusions; those who live in selflessness are willing to get to know someone slowly.
think: What does Prov 20:5 compare the human heart to?
When I get to know someone, am I quick to draw conclusions, or do I ask questions patiently?
What is one good question I can prepare today to get to know a friend’s heart?
lessons.speak: Lord, give me wisdom and patience, so that I can enter a person’s heart through good questions. Make me willing to listen and not hurry to speak, and help me respect other people’s boundaries. Guard my own heart too, so that I neither hand it over easily nor close it easily. Amen.
lessons.do: Today ask a friend a “deeper” question, such as: What is one lesson you have learned lately? Then just listen, without interrupting and without giving advice.
lessons.quick: Getting to know a person is patiently drawing water, not forcing an interrogation.
text: Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out.

lessons.title: Like a Tree Planted by the Streams of Water
lessons.hear:
Whenever Xiaoqi got to know someone, she worried that “the other person wasn’t good enough,” but she rarely thought about whether her own roots went deep enough. Later her mentor asked her, “Where do you drink from every day?” Only then did she realize that her life was propped up by other people’s affirmation, and that once no one responded, her heart felt empty.

The Psalms say, “He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water,” that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. (Ps 1:3) Good fruit does not come from straining hard, but from roots connected to living water. This water is God’s word, and closeness with God.

Getting to know others begins with knowing myself. Am I beside the streams of water? Do my quiet time, my fellowship, and my obedience let me bear fruit in its season? Only a person whose roots are planted in God has the ability to discern, and the ability to love. This is also the best preparation you can make for a relationship.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he often withdrew to quiet places to be with the Father, so he bore abundant fruit. The Bible is my standard: delight in the Lord’s law and meditate on it day and night. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he is the river of living water flowing out of me. Those who live for self strain to bear fruit; those who live in selflessness quietly stay beside the streams of water.
think: In Ps 1:3, what is the blessed person compared to?
Is my life right now planted beside the streams of water, or propped up by other people’s affirmation?
Today, how can I sink my roots deeper into God’s word?
lessons.speak: God, thank you for being the living water of my life. Let my roots go deep into your word, so that I do not live on other people’s affirmation. Let me bear fruit in its season, and let my leaf not wither, so that in my relationships I am also a blessing to others. Amen.
lessons.do: Today set a regular time to read Psalm 1, meditate on it slowly, and write one sentence: Today I want this word to enter my life.
lessons.quick: Good fruit comes from roots connected to living water, not from straining.
text: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;
but his delight is in the LORD’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.
He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.

lessons.title: Pursue Righteousness, Faith, Love, and Peace
lessons.hear:
Looking back on this week: knowing people by their fruits (Matt 7:16), what is stored in the heart (Luke 6:45), patiently drawing water (Prov 20:5), a tree planted by the streams of water (Ps 1:3).

Paul says to the young Timothy, “Flee from youthful lusts; but pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart.” (2 Tim 2:22) There are two actions here: fleeing and pursuing. Fleeing means leaving the environments and thoughts that make you stumble; pursuing means moving toward righteousness, faith, love, and peace together with those who have a pure heart.

Getting to know a person is not only observing; it is also pursuing together. Are you pursuing righteousness together? Are you drawing near to God together? This week, did you notice where you need to flee and where you need to pursue?

If you feel that in a relationship you are often controlled, humiliated, or afraid, please also reach out to people you trust and to professional organizations.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, and his fruit is love; the Bible is my standard, knowing people by their fruits; the Holy Spirit is my guide, letting me see the truth and be renewed. Those who live for self go by feelings; those who live in selflessness go by the Holy Spirit and the Bible. Let Jesus be King, and the glory goes to God.
think: Where did I see self this week? How did God support me in it?
According to 2 Tim 2:22, what are we to flee, and what are we to pursue?
What is one thing I will flee next week, and one thing I will pursue?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for this week of learning to know people and to know myself. Help me flee what makes me stumble, and give me courage to pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace together with those who have a pure heart. All the glory be to you. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal write: one thing I saw this week that I need to flee; one thing I will pursue; one partner I can pursue it with. Tell that partner about it today.
lessons.quick: Flee youthful lusts, and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with those who have a pure heart.
text: Flee from youthful lusts; but pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart.

weeks.keyText: By their fruits you will know them. Do you gather grapes from thorns or figs from thistles? Even so, every good tree produces good fruit, but the corrupt tree produces evil fruit. A good tree can’t produce evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree produce good fruit. Every tree that doesn’t grow good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. Therefore by their fruits you will know them.

weeks.title: Of One Heart, and Not Unequally Yoked
weeks.theme: Walking together requires walking in the same direction. It isn’t about picking at the other person; it’s about first asking, “Where are we headed?”
group: Read 2 Cor 6:14. What picture does “yoked together” bring to mind? Why do two people headed in different directions find the journey so exhausting?
In faith, values, and the direction of life, what are the things you can’t compromise on with your future partner?
This week, whom would you like to ask for advice about your own “non-negotiables list,” or what would you like to pray about? Ask your group members to pray for you.
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday service, talk with a mature companion and say, “I believe the three most important shared directions in a relationship are…” The other person can add to the list or offer a gentle reminder. Finally, pray over the list together.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, hold a “walking in the same direction” discussion with one or two trusted friends. It isn’t aimed at anyone in particular; it’s only about these questions: What am I willing to serve God in? How am I willing to treat money and time? What do I hope my family will look like? Each person writes down three sentences, and everyone listens to one another without debating.

lessons.title: Do Not Be Yoked Together with Unbelievers
lessons.hear:
Xiejie really liked a young man. He was kind, funny, and respectful toward her; he just had no interest in faith. She was torn inside: He’s so good. Am I overthinking this?

Paul says, “Don’t be unequally yoked with unbelievers, for what fellowship do righteousness and iniquity have? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness?” (2 Cor 6:14) A yoke is the crossbar placed on two oxen so they can pull a plow together. If the two oxen head in different directions or pull with different strength, the work becomes exhausting, and they may even hurt each other.

This verse does not tell us to look down on unbelievers, nor does it say they are bad people. It reminds us that in the closest, longest-lasting relationships, the direction of our lives decides everything. Faith is not a hobby; it is the foundation of the whole of life. You can love your unbelieving friends warmly, but when it comes to walking together in marriage, be careful. This is a matter to think through with prayer and with trusted companions.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he loved sinners and sat at table with them, yet he never went along with sin. The Bible is my standard: do not be yoked together with unbelievers. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives me wisdom to love people while guarding my faith. The self-centered make choices by feeling; the selfless let God’s direction guide the relationship.
think: What metaphor does 2 Cor 6:14 use to describe a mismatched relationship?
In my relationships, do I treat faith as a hobby or as the foundation of my life?
How can I love my unbelieving friends and still guard my own direction?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for loving me and for loving everyone who does not yet know you. Give me wisdom and courage so that, in my closest relationships, you remain at the center. Help me not to look down on others and not to treat my own faith lightly. May we walk together in your direction. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down three things on which, no matter what, you are unwilling to compromise in your faith. When you finish, pray over the list, and ask a mature companion to look it over with you.
lessons.quick: Faith is the foundation of life, not just a hobby.
text: Don’t be unequally yoked with unbelievers, for what fellowship do righteousness and iniquity have? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness?

lessons.title: Can Two Walk Together Unless They Agree?
lessons.hear:
Han and his girlfriend had been dating for six months. Both loved the Lord and loved serving. But they gradually discovered that one wanted to do overseas mission work while the other wanted to stay in their hometown and care for parents. Neither was willing to give way, and neither dared to talk it through properly.

Amos asks, “Do two walk together, unless they have agreed?” (Amos 3:3) Being of one heart does not mean thinking exactly alike. It means that, facing important directions, we are willing to seek God together and adjust to one another. Sometimes being of one heart is worked out slowly. At other times, we discover that our callings really are different.

This discovery is not a failure; it is honesty. Seeing it early is a kind of protection, compared with walking into a deeper relationship while heading in different directions. Talking about direction takes humility, prayer, and the company of people we trust. Don’t let avoidance take the place of conversation, and don’t let pressure take the place of respect.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he was one with the Father and said, “I and the Father are one.” The Bible is my standard: can two walk together unless they agree? The Holy Spirit is my guide: he helps us seek God’s will in the midst of our differences. The self-centered want the other person to fit their plans; the selfless join the other person in obeying God.
think: According to Amos 3:3, what does walking together require?
In which major directions have I not yet talked honestly with the important people in my life?
Today, how can I invite that person or a companion to talk about direction?
lessons.speak: Lord, give us one heart, not a forced sameness but a shared seeking of your will. Give me courage to talk honestly about direction, and humility to be adjusted by you. Keep me from hiding what truly matters out of fear of loss. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, say to a companion, “There is an important direction I most want to talk with you about.” Set a time, and pray beforehand for the conversation, asking God to give you honesty and gentleness.
lessons.quick: One heart doesn’t mean the same; it means seeking God’s will together.
text: Do two walk together, unless they have agreed?

lessons.title: A House Built on the Rock
lessons.hear:
Kai had attended many marriage seminars and filled many notebooks. He could talk eloquently about what makes a good relationship. But whenever his girlfriend criticized him, he went cold at once and said, “I don’t want to talk right now.” This reaction had repeated many times.

Jesus says, “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who built his house on the rock.” (Matt 7:24) Knowing is not the same as doing. Whether a relationship can stand depends not on how much we have heard but on how we actually live.

The storms will certainly come: conflict, misunderstanding, disappointment. A truly steady relationship is one where we practice listening and practice doing in small things, setting the foundation on the words of Christ. Don’t wait until a storm hits to discover there is no foundation. Starting today, in small things, hear and do.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his words and his life were completely one. The Bible is my standard: to hear and do is to build the house on the rock. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he helps me obey in small things and gives me strength to carry out his words. The self-centered only know; the selfless hear and do.
think: According to Matt 7:24, why did the wise man’s house stand?
In my relationships, what is one thing I clearly know I should do but haven’t done?
Today, what small thing can I start with, hearing and doing?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, forgive me for only knowing and not doing. Build the foundation of my life on your words, so that when the storms come, I can still stand firm. Holy Spirit, give me strength to begin with small things and to do what I hear. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose one small thing you clearly know you should do but have kept putting off, such as apologizing, tidying up, or saying one true thing, and do it right now. Don’t wait.
lessons.quick: To hear and do is to build a relationship on the rock.
text: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who built his house on the rock.
The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock.

lessons.title: A Woman Who Fears the LORD
lessons.hear:
Xin often felt she wasn’t pretty enough or attractive enough. Whenever she saw other people’s photos or other people’s romances, she told herself, I’m just not good enough. She had also seen many brothers who, in choosing a partner, looked only at appearance and seldom asked about the person’s heart.

Proverbs says, “Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain; but a woman who fears the LORD, she shall be praised.” (Prov 31:30) In its original context, this verse praises women, but the principle it reveals applies to brothers and sisters alike: looks change and circumstances shift, but what lasts is a life that fears the LORD.

You don’t need to be seen because of your appearance, and you don’t need to measure others by theirs. A person who fears God has wisdom, humility, honesty, and love. This kind of beauty does not fade with age. At the same time, remember that every person God has made has something worth appreciating.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he had no stately form or majesty, yet he had the most beautiful life. The Bible is my standard: those who fear the LORD will be praised. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives me a lasting beauty within and teaches me to appreciate the inner life of others. The self-centered prove their worth by appearance; the selfless are called precious before God.
think: According to Prov 31:30, which kind of beauty lasts?
Do I use looks or credentials to measure my own worth or that of others?
Today, how can I learn to appreciate someone’s inner life of fearing God?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for making me in your image. Heal my habit of comparing appearance and credentials, so that before you I know I am precious. Help me also to value a life that fears you. May my beauty come from fearing you. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, say to yourself, “I am made and loved by God.” Then say to one person a word that appreciates their inner character, for example, “I really admire your honesty.”
lessons.quick: Looks change; a life that fears God is beauty that lasts.
text: Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain; but a woman who fears the LORD, she shall be praised.

lessons.title: Your Word Is a Lamp to My Feet
lessons.hear:
Looking back on this week: not being yoked with unbelievers (2 Cor 6:14), walking together of one heart (Amos 3:3), the house built on the rock (Matt 7:24), and the beauty of fearing God (Prov 31:30).

The psalmist says, “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.” (Ps 119:105) This lamp does not light up the whole road; it lights up the step right in front of our feet. We don’t need to see the destination before we dare to set out; as long as we can see the next step, we can walk.

In relationships, God leads in the same way. His word shows us where we need to stop, where we need to wait, and where we can move forward. As we walk with others, we also read God’s word together, pray together, and obey together. This lamp will never lead anyone in the wrong direction.

This week, was there any place where you wanted to see clearly on your own without first reading God’s word?
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example; he is the light of the world. The Bible is my standard; it is the lamp to my feet. The Holy Spirit is my guide; he helps me see the next step before me. The self-centered want to see everything at once; the selfless follow one step at a time. Let Jesus be King, and all glory to God.
think: Where did I see my own self-centeredness this week? How did God support me in it?
According to Ps 119:105, what is God’s word to my feet?
Which passage will I read first next week as a light for my relationships?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that your word is a lamp to my feet. Forgive the pride of wanting to see everything clearly on my own. Help me follow you one step at a time, and in my relationships always seek your word first. All glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal, write down: the biggest discovery I made this week; the passage I will read first; and the companion I need to walk with me. Read that passage today, and pray about your next step.
lessons.quick: God’s word lights the step in front of us, and we follow one step at a time.
text: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.

weeks.keyText: Don’t be unequally yoked with unbelievers, for what fellowship do righteousness and iniquity have? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness?

weeks.title: Green Flags: Healthy Love
weeks.theme: Healthy love is honest, willing to seek counsel, and ready to be taught.
group: Prov 12:22 says what kind of people please God?
In your relationships, which green flag are you most sure of? Which needs the most strengthening?
This week, what small step would you like to take in honesty or in seeking counsel? Ask your group members to pray for you.
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday service, find a companion and share with each other one small thing from this week where you chose honesty. Then send a sentence to a friend: “Thank you for telling me the truth.”
weeks.weekend: With a friend or a small group, put together a “healthy relationship green flags list.” Write down the five things you believe matter most, and pray for one another.

lessons.title: Lying Lips Are an Abomination to the LORD
lessons.hear:
Xiaoen found out that Hao had said he was working overtime on the weekend, when he had actually gone out with friends. He said he was only afraid she would be upset. Xiaoen answered, “It’s okay,” but inside she began to doubt every word he said.

In the past few weeks, we talked about red flags and about order. This week, we start with green flags, that is, what healthy love looks like. The first green flag is honesty. The Bible says, “Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD” (Prov 12:22), and the other half of the same verse says, “but those who do the truth are his delight.”

A little lie often feels like consideration, but it ends up digging a hole in trust. Honesty doesn’t mean laying everything out, and it doesn’t mean speaking harshly. It means not speaking falsehood and not hiding facts that would hurt the relationship.

Healthy love lets both people dare to speak the truth and be able to receive the truth.

Today, don’t rush to examine the other person. Start with yourself: Am I a person who can be trusted?
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he is the truth, and he is full of grace. The Bible is my standard: those who do the truth are God’s delight. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he is the Spirit of truth, so we don’t need lies to protect ourselves. The self-centered lie to save face; the selfless tell the truth because their security is in God.
think: According to Prov 12:22, what does God abhor, and what is his delight?
Lately, have I told a small lie or hidden something because I was afraid the other person would be upset?
Today, how can I tell the truth in one small matter?
lessons.speak: Lord, you are the truth, and you are my refuge. Forgive me for the lies and the hiding I have done for the sake of face and safety. Give me courage to speak the truth, and gentleness to receive other people’s truth. May all my words carry love and honesty. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, find one small matter and honestly say the part you were going to hide or gloss over. If it involves someone else, first make sure it is safe to say.
lessons.quick: Honesty is the first green flag of healthy love.
text: Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who do the truth are his delight.

lessons.title: Speak Truth Each One with His Neighbor
lessons.hear:
Some people say a romance needs mystery, so there’s no need to say everything. But the Bible’s reminder is direct: “Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak truth each one with his neighbor” (Eph 4:25).

The reason is in the second half: “for we are members of one another.” If the members of a body deceive one another, it’s like a hand lying to the eye, and the whole body falls down.

The “neighbor” here includes the person you’re dating. Honesty is more than not speaking falsehood. It also means being willing to say your feelings, needs, and boundaries, and not making the other person guess. Fang always said “anything is fine” when she was dating, but inside she cared a great deal. The feelings piled up until, in one outburst, she said everything at once, and both of them were frightened.

Speaking the truth should be timely, loving, and said when the other person can hear it. Said early, it’s a small word; said late, it’s a great wound.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he always spoke clearly and plainly to people, and he never shamed them. The Bible is my standard: put away falsehood and speak truth, because we are members of one another. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he helps us say what needs to be said at the right time. The self-centered pile up resentment in silence; the selfless speak clearly, in a timely and gentle way.
think: According to Eph 4:25, why should we speak the truth?
Do I often say “anything is fine” when that isn’t how I feel inside?
What is one small matter where I can honestly say my feelings or needs today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, take away the falseness and people-pleasing in my heart. Help me honestly say my feelings, and respect the other person’s feelings too. Holy Spirit, guide me to use the right words at the right time. And keep me from hiding in my relationships any longer. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, say one of your feelings or needs in a sentence without blame, for example, “I need a little time to think.” If you aren’t dating anyone, practice with a friend.
lessons.quick: Speak the truth in a timely way, and with love.
text: Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak truth each one with his neighbor, for we are members of one another.

lessons.title: Love Truth and Peace
lessons.hear:
The prophet Zechariah delivers God’s word: “These are the things that you shall do: speak every man the truth with his neighbor” (Zech 8:16), and he adds that we are to execute judgment that brings peace. Truth and peace stand side by side in this verse.

Some people think honesty means saying, “I’m just a straight shooter,” with no regard for other people’s feelings. Others think peace means not arguing and not saying anything true. In fact, real peace is built on honesty; peace without honesty is only a temporary quiet.

After one conflict, Zhe and Yating were cold toward each other for three days. Then Zhe took the first step and said, “I’m not sure what I did that hurt you, but I want to hear it.” Only then did Yating speak. Once it was out in the open, the atmosphere actually relaxed.

A healthy relationship is not one without conflict. It is one where, after the conflict, the relationship is still there and the person is still respected.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he is the Prince of Peace, yet he never hid the truth for the sake of peace. The Bible is my standard: speak the truth with your neighbor and make peace. The Holy Spirit is my guide: the fruit he bears includes peace, and also gentleness. The self-centered either force or flee; the selfless let go of winning and losing and face the problem together.
think: How does Zech 8:16 tell us to speak?
In conflict, do I tend to blow up or to go silent and flee?
Today, how can I say one thing in a way that is both honest and peace-bringing?
lessons.speak: Lord, make me love truth and love peace. Let me not escape into silence or hurt people with words. By your Spirit, help me respect the other person and respect the facts, even in conflict. And make me a peacemaker. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, think back on your most recent small quarrel and write two sentences: one a fact, and one your feeling. You don’t have to send them to the other person; first sort them out before God.
lessons.quick: Peace without honesty is only a temporary quiet.
text: These are the things that you shall do: speak every man the truth with his neighbor. Execute the judgment of truth and peace in your gates,

lessons.title: Without Counsel, Plans Fail
lessons.hear:
Kai wanted to invite a sister from church on a date. He was very serious about it, so he thought it over again and again, told no one, decided the time and place by himself, and even prepared a gift. The result: she was startled and felt a lot of pressure.

Proverbs says, “Where there is no counsel, plans fail; but in a multitude of counselors they are established.” (Prov 15:22)

A romance is not a secret plan for two people to hide away, especially when things aren’t yet clear. Seeking counsel from trusted elders, companions, or a pastor is not handing over our right to decide; it is letting others help us see our blind spots.

One mark of a green flag is that the relationship can be seen in the light by family, friends, and spiritual companions, and the other person doesn’t ask you to keep it hidden or to distance yourself from the people around you.

If a relationship asks you to treat it as “our secret, just the two of us,” be especially alert.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: before major decisions, he withdrew to pray and listened to the voice of the Father. The Bible is my standard: in a multitude of counselors, plans are established. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he often reminds us through the words of brothers and sisters. The self-centered decide alone; the selfless gladly let others help them see.
think: According to Prov 15:22, what happens when there is no counsel?
Does anyone know about my current relationship or thoughts? Am I deliberately keeping people from knowing?
Whom can I invite to be my counsel companion?
lessons.speak: Lord, give me trustworthy companions, and make me humble enough to let others see my thoughts and plans. Keep me from hiding and from deciding alone, and help me walk in the light. And give me wisdom to discern who makes a good companion for the journey. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, pick a trusted friend or elder, tell him or her one question you have about your love life, ask for an opinion, and pray about it together.
lessons.quick: A healthy relationship can be seen in the light.
text: Where there is no counsel, plans fail; but in a multitude of counselors they are established.

lessons.title: Listen to Counsel and Receive Instruction
lessons.hear:
Looking back on this week: honesty (Prov 12:22), speaking the truth (Eph 4:25), truth and peace (Zech 8:16), seeking counsel (Prov 15:22), and being teachable (Prov 19:20).

Healthy love has these green flags: speaking the truth, speaking it in the light, willingness to seek counsel, and willingness to be taught. These green flags are not a checklist for picking a partner; they are above all a mirror for looking at ourselves.

Please turn back and ask yourself: Where did I see my own self-centeredness this week? Did I use lies to protect my face, silence to pile up resentment, or pride to reject a reminder? Then ask: How did God support me in it? Perhaps through a verse, a friend, or a gentle reminder.

If you are single, these green flags apply to your friends and family too; if you are dating, you can use them to make your relationship healthier.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example; he is the truth. The Bible is my standard; it teaches us to speak the truth. The Holy Spirit is my guide; he gives me courage to be honest. The self-centered protect themselves with lies and defensiveness; the selfless, in God, are openly honest. Let Jesus be King, and all glory to God.
think: Where did I see my own self-centeredness this week?
How did God support me in it?
In what matter will I choose honesty and teachability next week?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for this week’s light. I have seen my weakness, and I have seen your grace. Help me be more honest and more teachable in my relationships, and let your truth reign in my life. And help me grow day by day through being taught. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal, write down: the green flag that struck me most this week; one habit I want to change; and one person who reminded me, whom I want to thank. Then send that person a word of thanks.
lessons.quick: Green flags are a mirror for ourselves, and a direction for growth.
text: Listen to counsel and receive instruction, that you may be wise in your latter end.

weeks.keyText: Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who do the truth are his delight.

weeks.title: Red Flags: Warning Signals of Danger
weeks.theme: Love should never make a person afraid; when you see danger, you are allowed to protect yourself.
group: What reminder do Prov 22:24–25 give us?
What do you think is the difference between “love” and “control”?

This week, what is one thing you would like to do for your own safety or the safety of someone around you? Ask your group members to pray for you. (If there is immediate danger, please call an emergency or help line first.)
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday service, read this week’s help information together with a trusted companion, and ask each other, “If one day I need help, whom will I turn to?” Send a sentence to a friend: “I’m here; you are not alone.”
weeks.weekend: With a friend, make “my help list”: write down three trusted people and a help phone number, and remind each other never to face danger alone.

lessons.title: Do Not Befriend a Hot-Tempered Man
lessons.hear:
[Read this first] If you are being threatened, controlled, or subjected to violence right now, please make sure of your physical safety first. Leave the dangerous place, and deal with everything else slowly afterward. In Taiwan you can call 110 (police), 113 (the protection hotline), 119 (emergency rescue), or 1925 (the mental health hotline); please rely on official announcements for numbers and services. This is not your fault.

When Xiaowen’s boyfriend was in a bad mood, he would throw things, and afterward he would cry and apologize, saying it was all because he loved her so much. Xiaowen stopped daring to share her opinions, afraid he would get angry.

Proverbs says, “Don’t befriend a hot-tempered man. Don’t associate with one who harbors anger” (Prov 22:24). The direction the Bible gives here is not to endure but to keep your distance.

Last week we talked about green flags; this week we talk about red flags, the signals that remind us there may be danger. Changing the way you speak and act out of fear that the other person will get angry is one important signal. Love should never make a person afraid.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he protected the weak, and he also withdrew when there was danger. The Bible is my standard: do not befriend a hot-tempered or wrathful man. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes the unease in our hearts a warning, not something to be pushed down. Selflessness is not enduring without regard for safety; selflessness is bravely choosing peace in God.
think: How much distance does Prov 22:24–25 urge us to keep from a hot-tempered person?
Have I ever changed my thoughts or actions because I was afraid the other person would get angry?
Whom can I tell about my situation and ask to look at it with me?
lessons.speak: Lord, I need your protection and wisdom. If I or someone near me is living in fear, give us courage to walk out of danger and find someone we can trust. Help me know that I am loved by you and that I deserve to be treated well. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down one thing you have done because you were afraid the other person would get angry, and tell a trusted person (a friend, pastor, or counselor). If there is immediate danger, call a help line right away.
lessons.quick: Love should never make a person afraid; if you feel unsafe, protect yourself first.
text: Don’t befriend a hot-tempered man. Don’t associate with one who harbors anger,
lest you learn his ways and ensnare your soul.

lessons.title: A Hot-Tempered Man Abounds in Sin
lessons.hear:
Every time Zhe got into an argument, he would rush up to the other person and shout. Afterward he would say, “I just have a bad temper; you need to put up with me.” Xiaohui remembered Proverbs 29:22: “An angry man stirs up strife, and a wrathful man abounds in sin.” (Prov 29:22)

A hot temper is not a personality trait; it is a sin and a wound that needs to be faced. A person who truly wants to change will admit it, apologize, and seek help. A person who only says “you need to put up with me” is actually pushing the responsibility onto the other person.

Here are a few red flags to be aware of: One, controlling where you go and your phone. Two, isolating you from friends and family. Three, shaming or belittling you. Four, threatening to leave, to harm themselves, or to harm you. Five, apologizing after an outburst and then repeating it. These are not love, and they are not your fault.

Seeing red flags doesn’t mean you must decide right away, but you must find someone to look at it with you.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he is gentle and humble, and he never controlled people with fear. The Bible is my standard: a wrathful man abounds in sin. The Holy Spirit is my guide: the fruit he bears includes gentleness and self-control. The self-centered control others with anger; the selfless, in the Holy Spirit, learn self-control and also invite others to help.
think: According to Prov 29:22, what happens to a wrathful man?
In the relationships around me, has controlling, isolating, or shaming behavior appeared?
Whom can I tell about this first?
lessons.speak: Lord, help me tell love from control. If I am being hurt, give me strength to speak up; if I myself have anger, help me admit it and be willing to seek help. Heal us, and protect us. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, check honestly against the five red flags: has any of them appeared in your current relationship? Write it down, and schedule a time to talk with a trusted person.
lessons.quick: Rage and control are not love, and they are not your fault.
text: An angry man stirs up strife, and a wrathful man abounds in sin.

lessons.title: Him Who Loves Violence
lessons.hear:
Some people say, “He only hit you once; he didn’t mean it.” But the psalm says, “The LORD examines the righteous, but his soul hates the wicked and him who loves violence.” (Ps 11:5)

God hates violence. These words are a comfort to everyone who has been hurt: God sees your pain, and he stands on the side of the victim.

Violence is not an expression of love, and it can’t be brushed aside as “losing control of emotions.” Shoving, slapping, destroying property, and threats all need to be taken seriously, whether the other person is male or female, and however gentle they were before.

After Xiaolan was pushed down and hurt, she remembered the other person’s tears and didn’t dare call the police. Later a friend went with her to have her injuries documented and stood by her as she faced her family. She said, “So I’m not alone.”

You can ask for help, and you can leave. This is not betrayal; it is protecting life.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he saw the oppressed and spoke up for them. The Bible is my standard: God’s soul hates the one who loves violence. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he is the Comforter, who accompanies the wounded. Selfless people do not endure violence; by God’s love, they choose safety and justice.
think: According to Ps 11:5, what is God’s attitude toward him who loves violence?
Has my view of “violence” ever been shaped by “he didn’t mean it”?
Who around me can walk the next step with me?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you that you hate violence and that you see the wounded. Heal every heart that has been hurt, and let them know they are not alone. Give them courage and trustworthy companions, so that step by step they walk toward peace. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the help channels you know: 110, 113, 1925, and one friend or pastor you trust, and save their contact information in your phone.
lessons.quick: God hates violence and stands on the side of the wounded.
text: The LORD examines the righteous, but his soul hates the wicked and him who loves violence.

lessons.title: Defend the Weak and the Fatherless
lessons.hear:
Psalm 82:3–4 says, “Defend the weak, the poor, and the fatherless. Maintain the rights of the poor and oppressed.” It goes on, “Rescue the weak and needy. Deliver them out of the hand of the wicked.” (Ps 82:3–4)

This passage is spoken to those who have the power: when you see the weak oppressed, speak up for them. The church and brothers and sisters are not bystanders.

De discovered that his friend Xiaoling’s boyfriend often shamed her in text messages. At first he said nothing and only listened; later he went with her to see a pastor and a counselor. He said, “I can’t decide for her, but I can walk with her.”

When you see a friend in a red-flag relationship, don’t blame her with “Why haven’t you left yet?” Listen first, believe first, accompany first. And don’t confront the other person yourself, so as not to increase the danger.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he drew near to the oppressed and defended them. The Bible is my standard: rescue the weak and needy, and deliver them out of the hand of the wicked. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes us helpers to one another. The self-centered look on; the selfless are willing to accompany, and respect the victim’s choices.
think: According to Ps 82:3–4, how are we to treat the oppressed?
Have I ever met a friend in an unhealthy relationship? What did I do then?
How can I do a better job of listening to, believing, and accompanying them?
lessons.speak: Lord, make me a friend who can be trusted, who doesn’t judge or blame but simply accompanies. Give me wisdom to know when to speak, when to listen, and when to find a professional. Protect the wounded. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, send a caring message to a friend you are worried about: “I care about you. Whenever you want to talk, I’m here.” Don’t interrogate, and don’t make decisions for them.
lessons.quick: Don’t blame the wounded; listen first, believe first, accompany first.
text: “Defend the weak, the poor, and the fatherless. Maintain the rights of the poor and oppressed.
Rescue the weak and needy. Deliver them out of the hand of the wicked.”

lessons.title: A Prudent Man Sees Danger and Takes Refuge
lessons.hear:
Looking back on this week: keeping a distance (Prov 22:24–25), the danger of rage (Prov 29:22), God’s hatred of violence (Ps 11:5), and defending the oppressed (Ps 82:3–4).

Today’s verse says, “A prudent man sees danger and takes refuge; but the simple pass on, and suffer for it.” (Prov 27:12) Seeing danger and taking refuge is not cowardice; it is wisdom.

Leaving danger is permitted by the Bible. Forgiveness can be given first, even by one side alone, but trust has to be rebuilt through the other person’s true repentance and action. Staying doesn’t make you more spiritual, and leaving doesn’t mean you aren’t trusting God.

Ask yourself: Where did I see my own self-centeredness this week? Did I push fear down with silence, or say “I can handle it” out of pride? Then ask: How did God support me in it? He may have used a friend, a reminder, or a help hotline.

Please remember: being hurt is not your fault.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example; he cares for the wounded. The Bible is my standard; it teaches us to take refuge from danger. The Holy Spirit is my guide; he gives us courage to ask for help. The self-centered try to hold on by themselves; the selfless are willing to let others help, and are held up by God. Let Jesus be King, and all glory to God.
think: Where did I see my own self-centeredness this week?
How did God support me in it?
Whom will I talk to next? Which help line do I need to call?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that you are my refuge. Give me wisdom to see danger, courage to leave, and companions to walk with me. Heal every wounded heart, and let us know that in you we are safe. All glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: Take one concrete step toward getting help: save the help numbers, tell a trusted person, or schedule time with a pastor or counselor. If there is immediate danger, call 110 or 113 right away.
lessons.quick: Seeing danger and taking refuge is wisdom, not weakness.
text: A prudent man sees danger and takes refuge; but the simple pass on, and suffer for it.

weeks.keyText: Don’t befriend a hot-tempered man. Don’t associate with one who harbors anger, lest you learn his ways and ensnare your soul.

weeks.title: Seeking Counsel from God and from Companions
weeks.theme: First ask God for wisdom, then seek counsel from trusted companions.
group: Jas 1:5 says what we should do when we lack wisdom?
Who are your counselors? Is there anyone among them who dares to tell you the truth?
For which matter this week would you like to seek counsel from both God and your companions? Ask your group members to pray for you.
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday service, find a trusted companion and say to each other, “One thing I’m seeking wisdom about lately is…” and then pray together. Send a sentence to a friend: “Thank you for being willing to listen to me, and willing to tell me the truth.”
weeks.weekend: Set aside half a day with a companion for “counsel and prayer”: first pray quietly on your own, then share with each other, and finally test it together with three checks: Scripture, fruit, and the light.

lessons.title: If You Lack Wisdom, Ask God
lessons.hear:
Zhihao wanted to know whether he should start dating a friend he had known for six months. He asked ten people and got ten different answers, which only left him more confused. He said, “Whom should I listen to?”

James says, “But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.” (Jas 1:5)

Notice two phrases: “liberally” and “without reproach.” God doesn’t think our questions are foolish, and he doesn’t mind how many times we ask.

There is an order to seeking counsel: first go before God and ask for wisdom, then consult trusted companions. If it’s done the other way around, and we listen to a pile of opinions before remembering to pray, we often get more confused the more we hear.

Asking God for wisdom is not asking God to decide for us; it is asking for clear eyes to see the situation and to see ourselves.

Today, there’s no need to rush to an answer. First quiet your heart and ask God.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: before major decisions, he prayed to the Father all night. The Bible is my standard: if we lack wisdom, we ask the God who gives to all liberally and without reproach. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he is the Spirit of wisdom, who helps us see clearly. The self-centered rely on their own cleverness; the selfless ask God first, then listen to people.
think: According to Jas 1:5, how does God give wisdom?
In my recent questions about love, have I first gone before God to ask for wisdom?
For which decision will I ask God for wisdom today?
lessons.speak: Father, I lack wisdom; please give it to me liberally. Keep me from being hasty or panicked, and from relying only on my own cleverness. Help me be still before you, to see your heart and to see the truth about myself. And help me trust your timing. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, pray for ten minutes and ask God just one thing: “In this matter, what do you want me to see first?” Write down what you receive.
lessons.quick: First ask God for wisdom, then seek counsel from people.
text: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.

lessons.title: In a Multitude of Counselors, Plans Are Established
lessons.hear:
Last week we talked about seeking counsel (Prov 15:22). This week, we place it within the order of seeking advice: “Where there is no counsel, plans fail; but in a multitude of counselors they are established.” (Prov 15:22)

What makes a good counselor? One, someone who loves God and has a testimony in the Lord. Two, someone who speaks to you sincerely, not only saying what you want to hear. Three, someone who doesn’t decide for you but helps you see clearly. Four, someone who can keep your privacy. Five, someone with no selfish interest in your well-being.

Whenever Huizhen ran into a relationship problem, she asked only her best friend, who loved her most. Her friend always said, “You deserve better!” She felt comfortable, but she was also blinded. Later she also invited an older sister in the faith, who told her some things she didn’t want to hear.

Good counselors are several in number, of different ages and perspectives, and all take God’s word as the standard.

Remember, a counselor helps you see; a counselor does not decide for you.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he sent his disciples out two by two, and he was glad to have people with him. The Bible is my standard: in a multitude of counselors, plans are established. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he offers different perspectives through different members of the body. The self-centered look only for people who agree with them; the selfless also look for people who dare to tell the truth.
think: According to Prov 15:22, under what circumstances are plans established?
Are my current counselors people who only echo me, or do they also dare to tell me the truth?
Whom can I invite to become my counselor?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for giving me brothers and sisters. Make me willing to seek counselors and willing to hear the truth. Let the counselors I choose be people who love you, fear you, and love me. Keep me from depending on human voices, and let me still take your word as the standard. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, list your three current counselors and check each one’s age, perspective, and honesty. If one kind is missing, begin to pray and invite a fourth person.
lessons.quick: Good counselors are several in number, and all take God’s word as the standard.
text: Where there is no counsel, plans fail; but in a multitude of counselors they are established.

lessons.title: The Wise Listen to Counsel
lessons.hear:
After Cheng argued with his girlfriend, a friend said to him, “Have you thought that maybe you spoke too harshly?” Cheng immediately said, “You don’t understand; she started it.”

Proverbs 12:15 says, “The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but he who is wise listens to counsel.” (Prov 12:15)

The mark of a fool is not a lack of intelligence but that his own way seems right in his own eyes, so he feels no need for others. The mark of a wise person is that he listens.

Listening to counsel doesn’t mean doing whatever others say; it means letting their words enter my thinking, and then testing them with Scripture and prayer.

When someone gives you counsel, first say, “Thank you for telling me,” and then go back and think about it. If you want to argue back every time, perhaps that is exactly the place that needs to be lit up.

Only someone who listens to counsel leaves room for his life to grow. This is a gift of humility.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he humbly learned, and he humbly taught. The Bible is my standard: he who is wise listens to counsel. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes me willing to be adjusted. The self-centered say, “You don’t understand”; the selfless say, “Thank you for telling me.” Humility overcomes pride; only those who are willing to listen have wisdom.
think: According to Prov 12:15, what is the difference between a fool and a wise person?
Has anyone given me counsel lately that I wanted to argue with on the spot?
How can I respond in a way that shows I am willing to listen to counsel?
lessons.speak: Lord, take away my self-righteous heart. When others give me counsel, help me first listen, then think, then pray. Make me humble and teachable, neither defending myself nor despising others’ words. Make me a wise person who listens to counsel. Amen.
lessons.do: Think back on the most recent time someone gave you counsel and you wanted to argue, write down the main point they made, and ask before God, “Is there something in this that you want to tell me?”
lessons.quick: The wise listen to counsel, and humility makes us grow.
text: The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but he who is wise listens to counsel.

lessons.title: The Spirit of Truth Will Guide You
lessons.hear:
Zhihao had heard many opinions and had prayed, but he still had no “feeling.” He asked, “How can I know whether this is the Holy Spirit’s guidance?”

Jesus says, “However, when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak.” (John 16:13)

A mark of the Holy Spirit’s guidance is that “he will guide you into all truth,” so it never contradicts the Bible. He also does not speak from himself but speaks what he hears, so he glorifies Jesus rather than himself or any person.

There are three checks for discerning the Spirit’s guidance: One, is it consistent with the Bible? Two, does it bear the fruit of the Spirit (love, joy, peace, patience)? Three, can it be seen in the light by trusted people?

Having no “feeling” doesn’t mean there is no guidance. Sometimes guidance comes step by step, day by day, and not as a flash of lightning.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he acted by the Holy Spirit and was of one heart with the Father. The Bible is my standard: the Holy Spirit guides us into all truth. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he never contradicts the Bible, and he makes us more like Jesus. The self-centered chase feelings; the selfless obey the truth. Humility overcomes pride; only those who are willing to be guided walk steadily.
think: According to John 16:13, what will the Spirit of truth do?
Have I ever mistaken my own wishes for the voice of the Holy Spirit?
Which three checks can I use to discern?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, guide me into all truth. Help me not to go by feelings or by wishes, but only by your word and your leading. Keep me from being misled by my own voice, and help me obey Jesus and glorify Jesus. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, take one matter you are thinking about and write out an answer to each of the three checks (Scripture, fruit, the light), and then go over it with a counselor.
lessons.quick: The Spirit’s guidance never contradicts the Bible, and it makes us more like Jesus.
text: However, when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak. He will declare to you things that are coming.

lessons.title: Ask, and It Will Be Given You
lessons.hear:
Looking back on this week: asking for wisdom (Jas 1:5), finding counselors (Prov 15:22), listening to counsel (Prov 12:15), and relying on the Holy Spirit (John 16:13).

Today’s verse is: “Ask, and it will be given you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened for you.” (Matt 7:7–8) Asking is not placing an order with God; it is living in trust toward the Father. He is a good Father and gives us good things.

Sometimes God’s answer is “yes,” sometimes “wait,” and sometimes “not this one.” Whichever it is, it comes out of love.

Ask yourself: Where did I see my own self-centeredness this week? Did I decide on my own and refuse to listen to people, or did I use many opinions as a substitute for prayer? Then ask: How did God support me in it?

Whatever the answer is, the Father is a good Father.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example; he asked the Father. The Bible is my standard; it teaches us to ask, seek, and knock. The Holy Spirit is my guide; he helps us gain wisdom in the light. The self-centered rely on themselves or on people alone; the selfless ask God first and also listen to people. Let Jesus be King, and all glory to God.
think: Where did I see my own self-centeredness this week?
How did God support me in it?
For which matter will I keep asking, seeking, and knocking next week?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for being willing to hear my requests. Help me seek you every day, and help me face myself honestly and open up to others. Whatever your answer, I trust that you are a good Father. All glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal, write down: one matter I am asking about; my three counselors; and the time I will wait and pray. Then entrust the matter to God, and don’t worry about it any more today.
lessons.quick: Asking, seeking, and knocking is living in trust toward the Father.
text: “Ask, and it will be given you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened for you.
For everyone who asks receives. He who seeks finds. To him who knocks it will be opened.

weeks.keyText: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.

weeks.title: Speaking the Truth
weeks.theme: Honesty needs love, and love needs honesty.
group: Eph 4:15 says what is the purpose of speaking the truth?
Where do you find it hardest to be “honest without hurting”?
In which relationship this week would you like to practice speaking the truth in love? Ask your group members to pray for you.
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday service, find a companion and say to each other one sincere word of thanks or encouragement, with no “buts.” Send a sentence to a friend: “Thank you for telling me the truth when it mattered.”
weeks.weekend: Do a “speaking practice” with a friend: each of you picks one sentence that is usually hard to say, says it to the other with love and honesty, and gives each other feedback.

lessons.title: Speaking the Truth in Love
lessons.hear:
Some people think honesty means saying whatever comes to mind. Xiejie’s boyfriend often said, “I’m just telling the truth!” and then criticized her clothes, her work, and her family. Every time she heard it, she felt terrible about herself.

Paul says, “but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ.” (Eph 4:15) Honesty must be joined with love; neither can be missing. Truth without love becomes hurtful; love without truth becomes people-pleasing.

There are three tests for speaking the truth in love: One, is my motive to help the other person, or to vent my own feelings? Two, am I stating a fact, or passing judgment on the person? Three, have I left the other person room to respond?

The goal is to “grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ,” so that both people draw closer to Jesus, not so that one wins over the other.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he spoke the truth to people, yet he was full of grace and compassion. The Bible is my standard: speak the truth in love, so that we grow in all things. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes my words both true and gentle. The self-centered attack with the truth or keep the peace with silence; the selfless speak the truth in love.
think: According to Eph 4:15, what attitude should go with speaking the truth?
Is my habit more like “speaking the truth regardless of feelings,” or “not speaking the truth for the sake of peace”?
Today, how can I say one true thing in a loving way?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are full of grace and full of truth. Teach me to speak the truth in love, neither hurting people nor pleasing them. Let every word I say bring people closer to you, and let me grow in love as well. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, pick one true thing you want to say to someone, run it through the three tests first, and then say it or write it using the pattern “I feel…, and I hope…”
lessons.quick: Honesty joined with love is healthy speech.
text: but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ,

lessons.title: The Wounds of a Friend Are Faithful
lessons.hear:
Proverbs 27:5–6 says, “Better is open rebuke than hidden love. The wounds of a friend are faithful, although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.” (Prov 27:5–6)

The “wounds” here are not violence but the face-to-face reminder of a faithful friend, which may make a person uncomfortable for a moment but comes out of love. By contrast, “kisses” stand for sweet talk and saying only what is pleasant to hear, which may be false.

Xiaofan, a friend of Xin’s, saw that Xin was giving too much to the person she was dating and bravely said, “I’m really worried about you. You seem less and less like yourself.” Xin was angry at first, but later she understood that this was a true friend.

Here is how to tell a true friend: Does he tell you to your face, or talk about you behind your back? Does he stay with you after he has spoken? Do his words come from love, or from looking down on you?

Practice being that kind of friend, too.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he laid down his life for his friends, and he also pointed out their blind spots to their faces. The Bible is my standard: the wounds of a friend are faithful. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes me willing to listen and also brave enough to speak. The self-centered love sweet words; the selfless treasure faithful reminders. Only selflessness can treasure a reminder.
think: According to Prov 27:5–6, what kind of wounds are faithful?
Do I have a friend like this around me? Do I treasure him?
Whom do I need to thank, or to whom do I need to say an honest word?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for giving me faithful friends. Help me treasure their reminders and not reject them because they sting. And make me that kind of friend, with love and with courage, willing to say what needs to be said for the other person. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, thank a friend who has told you the truth in the past. Tell him how that one sentence helped you, and ask him to keep reminding you.
lessons.quick: Faithful wounds are more precious than sweet words.
text: Better is open rebuke than hidden love.
The wounds of a friend are faithful, although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.

lessons.title: An Honest Answer Is Like a Kiss
lessons.hear:
Proverbs 24:26 says, “An honest answer is like a kiss on the lips.” (Prov 24:26) In ancient times, a kiss was a sign of sincere friendship. The meaning is that answering others with honest words is like offering a gift of genuine closeness.

Honest words sometimes take courage: saying “I disagree,” saying “I can’t do this,” saying “I need more time.” Words like these may disappoint the other person, yet they are a form of respect.

Xiaoqi was used to saying yes to everyone, worried that saying no would upset people. After a while, she didn’t even know what she wanted. Later she practiced saying, “Thank you for the invitation; I won’t go this time.” She found that her friends didn’t leave; they actually trusted her more.

Speaking honestly can protect the relationship, and it protects you.

Remember, being honest is not the same as being cold; it is genuine closeness.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he said yes when he meant yes and no when he meant no. The Bible is my standard: an honest answer is like a kiss on the lips. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes our words clear and gentle. The self-centered say untrue things to please people; the selfless are upright before God, and so they dare to speak the truth.
think: What does Prov 24:26 compare an honest answer to?
When is it hardest for me to say “no” to someone?
In which small matter today can I say something honestly and gently?
lessons.speak: Lord, help me speak honestly, not afraid of offending and not quick to hurt. Let my “yes” be “yes” and my “no” be “no,” said with respect and with love. Make me a person who can be trusted. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, practice saying one gentle “no” or “I need to think about it,” and notice how you feel. If you need to, practice with a friend first.
lessons.quick: Honest words are respect, and they are protection.
text: An honest answer is like a kiss on the lips.

lessons.title: Let Your Speech Be Seasoned with Salt
lessons.hear:
Paul says, “Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one.” (Col 4:6)

Salt does two things: it seasons, and it preserves. Speech seasoned with salt should make people able to take it in, and keep people from spoiling.

Speech with grace is not a fake smile; it leaves room in tone, timing, and choice of words. The same sentence heard in the morning or in the middle of the night, said in person or sent in a text, can have very different results.

When Sen and his girlfriend argued, they were in the habit of discussing it by text. Later they agreed: important matters would not go by text; they would be said face to face, and they would pray first. As a result, the arguments dropped a great deal.

Good words are not only in the content but also in the manner. Seasoning with salt is a way of living that thinks of the other person.

Today, let your words be like a little salt, just right.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his words were full of grace, bringing comfort and also bringing repentance. The Bible is my standard: speech with grace, seasoned with salt. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he bears the fruit of gentleness and self-control. The self-centered only want to get the words out; the selfless first think about how the other person will hear them.
think: According to Col 4:6, what should our speech be like?
When I say something important, what time do I usually choose and in what way?
Today, how can I add a little more salt to my words?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, make my speech full of grace, seasoned with salt. Before I speak, help me think about how the other person will hear it. Teach me to choose the right time and way, so that my words become a blessing and not a harm. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, before you say something important, stop and pray, and ask yourself: Does this come out of love? Is the timing right? Is the way right? Then decide how to say it.
lessons.quick: Good words are not only in the content but also in the manner.
text: Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one.

lessons.title: Rash Words Pierce Like a Sword
lessons.hear:
Looking back on this week: speaking the truth in love (Eph 4:15), the faithful wounds of a friend (Prov 27:5–6), an honest answer (Prov 24:26), and speech seasoned with salt (Col 4:6).

Today’s verse says, “There is one who speaks rashly like the piercing of a sword, but the tongue of the wise heals.” (Prov 12:18) Words have power: they can hurt, and they can heal.

Take a moment to think: What words have you spoken lately that were like a sword? And think, too: whose words have been like good medicine to you? If you have said hurtful words, you can go and apologize; if you have been hurt by words, remember that it was not your fault.

Ask yourself: Where did I see my own self-centeredness this week? Did I hold things down with silence, or hurt people with haste? Then ask: How did God support me in it?

The power of words is often greater than we think.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example; his words bring healing. The Bible is my standard; it teaches us to speak the truth in love. The Holy Spirit is my guide; he makes our speech seasoned with salt. The self-centered speak rashly; the selfless speak words that are like medicine to heal. Let Jesus be King, and all glory to God.
think: Where did I see my own self-centeredness this week?
How did God support me in it?
In which relationship will I speak one healing word next week?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for healing me with your words. Forgive me for the hurtful words I have spoken, and heal the wounds I have received. Make my tongue a healing medicine for others, and make my words bring life and hope. All glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal, write down: the sentence I said that was most like a sword, and the sentence I heard that was most like good medicine. Then give one medicine-like sentence to someone today.
lessons.quick: Words can wound, and words can become healing medicine.
text: There is one who speaks rashly like the piercing of a sword, but the tongue of the wise heals.

weeks.keyText: but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ,

weeks.title: Listening
weeks.theme: Be quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to anger.
group: What does Proverbs 18:13 say happens when we answer before we have heard?
What does it feel like to be truly heard in a relationship?
In which relationship do you want to practice better listening this week? Ask your group to pray for you.
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, find a partner. Each of you takes five minutes to talk while the other only listens, without interrupting or giving advice, and then says, “Thank you for telling me.” Send one sentence to a friend: “I’d like to hear from you. Would you tell me?”
weeks.weekend: Do a “ten minutes of focused listening” exercise with a partner: one speaks and one listens, using only “mm-hmm” and restating what you heard, and then you switch. Afterward, share how it felt to be heard.

lessons.title: Answering Before Hearing
lessons.hear:
Xiaoting had just begun to say, “Today I…” when Hao jumped in: “I know, you’re upset about that thing again.” Xiaoting paused and swallowed her words. Conversations like this happen every day in many relationships.

Proverbs says, “He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him.” (Prov 18:13)

Listening is not waiting for the other person to finish so it can be my turn. True listening gives the other person my full attention, without rushing to fix, defend, or advise.

Much of the hurt in relationships comes not from saying too little, but from listening too little. When people feel heard, they are often already half comforted.

Start with one small thing today: when someone is speaking, let them finish completely, pause for three seconds, and only then speak.

Remember, being heard is the beginning of love.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he often listened first, then asked, then responded. The Bible is my standard: answering before hearing is folly and shame. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives us ears to hear and hearts with room to receive. The self-centered person is eager to express himself; the selfless person lets the other be heard first. Only selflessness can listen.
think: What does Proverbs 18:13 say answering before hearing is?
Do I often interrupt others, or prepare a rebuttal in my head while they talk?
What can I do today to let one person truly be heard by me?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the best listener. Give me a heart that is willing to listen, not in a hurry to answer or defend myself. Help me listen with my ears and my heart to what others really want to say. Heal my habit of impatience. Amen.
lessons.do: When you talk with someone today, wait until they finish, pause for three seconds, and then restate their meaning in your own words: “What you mean is… Is that right?”
lessons.quick: True listening gives your full attention to the other person.
text: He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him.

lessons.title: The Heart of the Discerning Gets Knowledge
lessons.hear:
Proverbs 18:15 says, “The heart of the discerning gets knowledge. The ear of the wise seeks knowledge.” (Prov 18:15)

The discerning get knowledge with the “heart,” and the wise seek knowledge with the “ear.” In other words, listening is an active search, not passive waiting.

In dating, we often assume we already know what the other person is thinking. But people change, feelings change, and needs change. Only by actively listening can we know the other person’s real heart right now.

Fang assumed her boyfriend didn’t like sweets, so she never bought dessert. Only when she finally asked did she learn that he was just worried about gaining weight and actually wanted some. They both laughed.

Listen through questions: “How was your day?” “I’d like to understand more about what you just said.” Good questions draw a relationship closer.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he asked people many questions, such as “What do you want me to do for you?” The Bible is my standard: the ear of the wise seeks knowledge. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives us a curious heart to see what others are really like. The self-centered person assumes he already knows; the selfless person is willing to ask.
think: What does Proverbs 18:15 say the wise use to seek knowledge?
Do I assume I already understand the important people around me?
What sincere question can I ask someone today?
lessons.speak: Lord, make me humble, not assuming I already know everything. Help me seek knowledge with my ears and show care through my questions. Teach me to listen more and ask more, so that the people I love feel seen and understood. Make me willing to learn. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, ask someone near you an open-ended question, such as, “Has anything made you especially happy or worried lately?” Then just listen, without interrupting.
lessons.quick: Listen through good questions, and draw the relationship closer.
text: The heart of the discerning gets knowledge. The ear of the wise seeks knowledge.

lessons.title: Do Not Be Wise in Your Own Eyes
lessons.hear:
In Romans 12:16, Paul writes, “Be of the same mind one toward another. Don’t set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble. Don’t be wise in your own conceits.” (Rom 12:16)
