Thinking we are wise is the biggest obstacle to listening. When we feel, “I already know,” we cannot take anything in. When we feel, “I have more experience,” we easily look down on others.

Zhe often told his girlfriend, “I understand these things better than you.” Over time she stopped sharing her thoughts, because it made no difference. Zhe thought the relationship was calm, but she had already closed her heart.

Humility is returning to our proper place: I do not know everything, and I need others. Associating with the humble also means being willing to listen to those who are younger, weaker, or less experienced than I am.

Humility overcomes pride, and humility inspires humility.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he is God, yet he took the form of a servant and associated with the humble. The Bible is my standard: do not be wise in your own conceits. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes me willing to listen and willing to learn. The self-centered person exalts himself; the selfless person lets others be seen. Only selflessness can humbly receive instruction.
think: According to Romans 12:16, how should we not see ourselves?
When am I most likely to say, “I understand this better than you”?
From whom, someone I usually look down on, can I learn one thing?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, forgive my pride of thinking I am wise. Make me humble, willing to listen and willing to learn. Keep me from looking down on the lowly, or on those younger or less experienced than I am. Let me gain wisdom from you. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, ask someone you don’t usually turn to for advice about one thing. Sincerely thank them for sharing, and tell them what you learned.
lessons.quick: Humility makes us willing to listen and willing to learn.
text: Be of the same mind one toward another. Don’t set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble. Don’t be wise in your own conceits.

lessons.title: The One Who Has Knowledge Spares His Words
lessons.hear:
Proverbs 17:27 says, “He who spares his words has knowledge. He who is even tempered is a man of understanding.” (Prov 17:27)

A person with knowledge is not the one who speaks the most, but the one who knows when to speak and when not to. Restraining our words is not suppressing ourselves; it is making a choice.

In relationships, we often say the harshest things when emotions run high. “Let’s break up!” “You don’t love me at all!” Once spoken, such words cannot be taken back.

Xuan learned a habit: when he was so angry that he wanted to say something harsh, he would first say, “I need twenty minutes to cool down. Let’s talk again in a bit.” Then he would leave, pray, drink some water, and take a walk. When he came back, he could often say something better.

A pause is not avoidance, as long as you say clearly when you will return. A pause is for a better conversation.

If the other person would threaten you or hurt you more because you paused, put safety first and seek help.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: when he was reviled, he did not revile in return, and he spoke only when it was needed. The Bible is my standard: he who spares his words has knowledge, and he who is even tempered is a man of understanding. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives the fruit of self-control. The self-centered person speaks when emotions run high; the selfless person stops first in the Spirit.
think: According to Proverbs 17:27, what does the one who spares his words have?
When my emotions run high, what is the harshest sentence I most often say?
What sentence can I use to announce a pause?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, give me the fruit of self-control. When my emotions run high, help me stop first and not say hurtful words. Help me be quiet, pray, and then speak my heart with gentle words. Make me an even-tempered person of understanding. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, agree with a partner on a pause sentence, such as, “I need twenty minutes, and I will come back.” Then think about how you will calm down.
lessons.quick: A pause is not avoidance; it is for a better conversation.
text: He who spares his words has knowledge. He who is even tempered is a man of understanding.

lessons.title: Quick to Hear
lessons.hear:
Look back over this week: listen before answering (Prov 18:13), seek knowledge with the ear (Prov 18:15), do not be wise in your own conceits (Rom 12:16), and spare your words (Prov 17:27).

James says, “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger; for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.” (Jas 1:19–20)

Being quick to hear is active; being slow to speak is a choice; being slow to anger is self-control. These three things sum up this whole unit on listening.

Ask yourself: where did I see my self-centeredness this week? Was it interrupting others, rushing to prove myself, or assuming I already knew? Then ask: how did God support me in it?

Listening is another way of saying love. When we are willing to listen, we are saying, “You matter to me.”
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, and he was quick to hear; the Bible is my standard, teaching us to be slow to speak and slow to anger; the Holy Spirit is my guide, giving us self-control. The self-centered person is quick to speak; the selfless person is quick to hear. Let Jesus be King, and all glory to God.
think: Where did I see my self-centeredness this week?
How did God support me in it?
In which relationship will I choose to be quick to hear next week?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for always listening to me. Teach me to follow your way, to be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger. Make me someone who is willing to listen and can be trusted in every relationship. All glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal, write down: the time this week I listened best, and the time I interrupted someone. Then choose someone important to you and listen to them attentively for ten minutes today.
lessons.quick: Listening is another way of saying love, and a way of showing respect.
text: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;
for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.

weeks.keyText: He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him.

weeks.title: Conflict: How to Argue
weeks.theme: Conflict is nothing to fear; handled with love, order, and humility, it can bring us closer.
group: What does Matthew 18:15 say to do when someone sins against you?
What is the most common kind of conflict in your relationships?
What is one thing you want to practice this week in handling conflict? Ask your group to pray for you. (If violence or threats are involved, please seek help first.)
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, find a partner and share with each other, “The most recent time I resolved a conflict.” Then pray together. Send one sentence to a friend: “Thank you for being willing to talk things through with me.”
weeks.weekend: Practice the four steps of “pause, listen, speak, decide” with a partner: each of you picks a small-argument scenario, act it out once, and give each other feedback.

lessons.title: If He Listens, You Have Gained Your Brother
lessons.hear:
First, a clear word: the method in this lesson is for ordinary conflicts and misunderstandings. It is not for relationships involving violence, threats, or control. If you feel unsafe, go back to Week 34, protect yourself first, and seek help. Do not confront the person alone.

Jesus said, “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.” (Matt 18:15)

The order in this verse is: first in private, then in conversation, and the goal is to “gain” the other person, not to beat them. Many people do the opposite: they first complain to others, or vent in a group chat, and only at the end speak to the person involved.

Xiaoqi was very unhappy about her boyfriend’s lateness. She first said a lot about it in front of her friends, and only then talked to him face to face. He felt he had been talked about behind his back, and became even more defensive.

Go to the person first, with love, aiming to restore the relationship.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he taught us to deal with conflict directly, privately, and with love. The Bible is my standard: show him his fault between you and him alone. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he keeps us from rushing to blame and leads us to seek reconciliation. The self-centered person wants to win; the selfless person wants to gain the other person.
think: According to Matthew 18:15, what is the first step when someone sins against you?
Is my habit to tell others first, or to go straight to the person?
How can I go to someone with love today and talk about one small matter?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, give me wisdom and courage to handle conflict the way you taught. Keep me from talking behind anyone’s back or bottling things up inside. Let my goal be to gain my brother, not to beat him. Guard my heart and fill it with love. Amen.
lessons.do: If you have a small misunderstanding with someone, and it is safe, pray first today, then arrange a private talk with them, beginning with “I feel…” If it is not safe, first talk it over with someone you trust.
lessons.quick: Go to the person privately; the goal is to gain them, not to beat them.
text: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.

lessons.title: The Beginning of Strife Is Like Breaching a Dam
lessons.hear:
Cheng and his girlfriend started arguing over something small, and the longer they went on, the louder they both got. Finally he said, “You always do this!” and she said, “You don’t care about me at all!” What began as a question about a goodnight text turned into a big debate over whether they were right for each other.

Proverbs says, “The beginning of strife is like breaching a dam, therefore stop contention before quarreling breaks out.” (Prov 17:14)

Once the water is let loose, it is hard to take back. Contention must be stopped at the very beginning.

Some early signals: a raised voice, bringing up old issues, words like “every time,” “never,” and “you always,” and speech turning sarcastic. When you see these signs, it is time to stop.

Say, “Let’s stop for a moment. I want to listen to you properly.” This sentence is often more powerful than any argument.

Remember, stopping is not losing; it is protecting each other.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he calmed the storm, and he calms hearts. The Bible is my standard: stop contention before quarreling breaks out. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives the fruit of peace. The self-centered person lets the water keep flowing; the selfless person shuts the floodgate at the very start. Only selflessness can let go of winning and losing.
think: What does Proverbs 17:14 compare the beginning of strife to?
Which early signal shows up most often in my arguments?
What sentence can I use to stop at the very beginning of an argument?
lessons.speak: Lord, give me a heart of peace. When we start to argue, remind me to stop first. Keep me from bringing up old issues, from saying “every time,” and from saying hurtful words. Let our disagreements become a chance to know each other better. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of a “stop” sentence with a partner, and write down your three most common “early signals.” Use it the next time they appear.
lessons.quick: Stop an argument at the very beginning; the earlier, the better.
text: The beginning of strife is like breaching a dam, therefore stop contention before quarreling breaks out.

lessons.title: Better Than Taking a City
lessons.hear:
Proverbs 16:32 says, “One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city.” (Prov 16:32)

In ancient times, a warrior took pride in conquering cities. But the Bible says that one who can rule his own heart is stronger than one who takes a city.

Many people think beating the other person is victory. But in a relationship, you can win the debate and lose the relationship. True victory is ruling your own heart: my anger, my pride, my desire to prove I am right.

When Kai and his girlfriend disagreed, he used to win by being louder. Later he learned to admit first, “I have my own shortcomings.” His girlfriend’s attitude softened too.

In the Holy Spirit, we receive the strength to rule our own hearts. This is the victory of selflessness, not someone else’s defeat.

Remember, true victory is a win for both.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: on the cross he overcame himself, and he overcame sin and death. The Bible is my standard: one who rules his spirit is better than one who takes a city. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives the strength of self-control. The self-centered person wants to beat the other; the selfless person lets humility overcome pride, and both win.
think: According to Proverbs 16:32, what is better than the mighty?
In a conflict, what do I want to win: the argument, or face?
In what situation today can I choose to rule my own heart?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, help me rule my own heart. When I want to win the argument, make me quiet first; when I want to raise my voice, make me listen first. Let my victory be not over a person, but over my own pride. Amen.
lessons.do: The next time you feel like arguing, take a deep breath first and pray, “Lord, I want to overcome myself, not him.” Then choose a gentler response.
lessons.quick: One who rules his spirit is better than the mighty, and better than one who takes a city.
text: One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city.

lessons.title: Where Do Your Fights Come From?
lessons.hear:
James asks a direct question: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” (Jas 4:1–2)

The surface causes of many conflicts are time, money, division of tasks, or family. But the Bible points deeper: inside us are some “I want” desires, and when they go unmet they turn into battles.

Xiaopei and her boyfriend argued for a long time over who would give way on the weekend. Later she realized that what she really wanted was to “be valued.” When she said that need out loud, the shape of the argument changed.

Ask yourself: behind this conflict, what do I really want? To be respected, accompanied, affirmed, or to be in control? Only when we see our desires do we have a chance to hand them over to God.

Self-centered desires that are not entrusted to God turn into demands on other people.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he always entrusted his needs to the Father. The Bible is my standard: fights come from the desires that war within us. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he lets us see our heart’s real needs. The self-centered person demands that others meet his needs; the selfless person entrusts needs to God and also tells people honestly.
think: According to James 4:1–2, where do fights come from?
In my most recent conflict, what did I really want?
Which need can I first entrust to God?
lessons.speak: Lord, search my heart, and let me see my real needs and desires. I am willing to give them to you. Help me not to fight to get what I want, but to ask and trust you, and to tell the one I love honestly. Amen.
lessons.do: Think back to your most recent argument and write down: the surface cause, and the real need behind it. If it is fitting, say one sentence to the other person: “What I actually need is…”
lessons.quick: Behind a conflict there is often an unseen need.
text: Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?
You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war. You don’t have, because you don’t ask.

lessons.title: It Is His Glory to Overlook an Offense
lessons.hear:
Look back over this week: go to the person privately first (Matt 18:15), stop contention at the beginning (Prov 17:14), rule your own heart (Prov 16:32), and see the desires behind the conflict (Jas 4:1–2).

Today’s verse says, “The discretion of a man makes him slow to anger. It is his glory to overlook an offense.” (Prov 19:11)

Overlooking an offense is not indulging it. It means not holding on to small things; the problems that need to be faced still have to be handled honestly. But for small matters that are not issues of principle, we can let go, and that too is our glory.

Ask yourself: where did I see my self-centeredness this week? Was it rushing to win, bringing up old issues, or holding on to someone’s small mistakes? Then ask: how did God support me in it?

If what you are facing is violence or threats, overlooking an offense is not the answer; go back to Week 34 and protect yourself first.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, and he was patient with human weakness; the Bible is my standard, teaching us to handle conflict in the right order; the Holy Spirit is my guide, making us slow to anger. The self-centered person holds on to offenses; the selfless person lets go in God. Humility inspires humility, and both win. Let Jesus be King, and all glory to God.
think: Where did I see my self-centeredness this week?
How did God support me in it?
What new approach will I choose in a conflict next week?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for overlooking my offenses. Teach me to be patient with others too, and honest about what needs to be faced. Let my conflicts become chances to draw closer. However we argue, build us up in each other. All glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal, write down: one improvement in how I handled conflict this week; one small thing I will let go of; one thing that needs to be faced honestly. Then take one small action: apologize, thank someone, or ask for a talk.
lessons.quick: Overlooking an offense is glory, but face honestly what must be faced.
text: The discretion of a man makes him slow to anger. It is his glory to overlook an offense.

weeks.keyText: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.

weeks.title: Apology and Forgiveness
weeks.theme: Forgiveness can be given by me first; an apology is taking responsibility, not making excuses.
group: Read Colossians 3:13. How did the Lord forgive us? How should we forgive others?
What is the difference between forgiving and trusting again? How have you mixed them up in the past?
Whom do you need to apologize to this week, or what hurt do you need to hand over to God? Ask your group to pray for you.
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, with a trustworthy partner, each say one sentence: “One thing I need to entrust to God is…” and then pray for each other. When you get home, send one sentence to a friend: Forgiveness can be given first; trust depends on change.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, arrange a time with a trustworthy partner to read Matt 6:14–15 and Luke 17:3–4 together. Each of you writes down “what I need to forgive” and “what I need to take responsibility for,” and then pray for each other. You do not need to share details. If personal safety is involved, please go to a pastor or professional first, or call the 113 protection hotline.

lessons.title: As the Lord Forgave You, So You Also Do
lessons.hear:
Xiaojie and her boyfriend broke up six months ago, yet every time she remembers the night he humiliated her in front of their friends, her chest still tightens. Friends at church told her, “You need to forgive him.” But to her, forgiving felt like being asked to pretend nothing had happened.

Paul says, “even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.” (Col 3:13) The standard of forgiveness is the Lord’s forgiveness. When the Lord forgives us, he does not say, “It was nothing.” He pays the price and bears the sin himself.

So forgiveness is not pretending we were not hurt, and it is not saying the harm does not matter. It is handing over my right to collect the debt to God, and no longer letting resentment rule me. Forgiveness can be given first, by me alone. Trusting again is a different matter; it depends on whether the other person has truly changed. This week, we will learn to tell these two things apart.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: on the cross he asked forgiveness for others, yet he never said the harm did not exist. The Bible is my standard: as the Lord forgave you, so you also do. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives me strength to let go of resentment. The self-centered person clings to what the other owes and wants to be the judge; the selfless person hands judgment to God, letting people be people and God be God.
think: According to Colossians 3:13, what is the standard for how we forgive others?
Is there something in my heart that I have mistaken for “I must pretend nothing happened” in order to forgive?
Which hurt am I willing to hand over to God today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for forgiving me first. Help me see clearly whose debt I am still holding on to. Holy Spirit, give me strength to hand this over to you, without pretending nothing happened and without letting resentment rule me. I want to learn to forgive the way you forgive. Amen.
lessons.do: Write down one thing that hurt you, and after it write: “I hand this over to God.” Read it aloud once. If you cannot do that yet, write instead: “Lord, I am willing. Please help me.”
lessons.quick: Forgiveness can be given by me first; trust waits for the other person’s real change.
text: bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.

lessons.title: If You Forgive Men Their Trespasses
lessons.hear:
Some people read this passage and are startled: if I don’t forgive, will God not forgive me? So they force themselves to say, “I forgive,” while their hearts churn even more.

This follows right after the Lord’s Prayer. Jesus said, “For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.” (Matt 6:14) The point is not a transaction but the shape of a life: a person who has truly received God’s forgiveness has a softened heart, while a person who clings to resentment grows hard, and so blocks himself from receiving grace.

Forgiveness is a process. Letting go a little today and being triggered again tomorrow does not mean failure. You can say to God, “I am willing to forgive. Please help me.” What God values is a willing heart, and your coming to him honestly, one step at a time.

But remember: forgiving does not mean going back into a relationship that harms you.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he taught us to pray, and he taught us to forgive. The Bible is my standard: if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he softens my heart little by little. The self-centered person protects himself with resentment; the selfless person lets Christ’s grace be his protection.
think: According to Matthew 6:14, how is forgiving others connected to the Father’s forgiveness?
Am I forcing myself to say I have forgiven because I am afraid?
What honest sentence can I say to God: “I can’t yet, but I am willing”?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for forgiving my many trespasses. I admit there are things I still cannot let go of, and people I still resent. Soften my heart so that I am willing to forgive little by little, and help me tell the difference between forgiving and returning to an unsafe place. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal, write three sentences: what hurt me; what I am willing to hand over to God; what I still need God’s help with. Then pray about it for one minute.
lessons.quick: Forgiveness is a process, and God values a willing heart.
text: “For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.
But if you don’t forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

lessons.title: If He Repents, Forgive Him
lessons.hear:
Xiaowei’s boyfriend kept lying. Each time he was found out, he said he was sorry, but a few days later it was the same again. She was torn: doesn’t the Bible say to forgive seven times?

Jesus said, “If he repents, forgive him.” (Luke 17:3) There is an order here: when someone sins against you, you may point it out; when the other person repents, that is, truly turns around, the relationship can move forward. The Lord Jesus also said that even if he turns back seven times in a day, you shall forgive him (Luke 17:4).

But this is not telling you to endure the same harm again and again. A heart of forgiveness should always be ready; yet rebuilding a relationship depends on whether the other person has truly turned and changed. If the other person is controlling, threatening, or violent, do not go to rebuke him alone. First find trusted people and professionals, and protect your own safety.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he opens his arms to those who repent, yet he does not let sin be brushed aside. The Bible is my standard: if he repents, forgive him. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he helps me discern what true repentance is. The self-centered person either holds a grudge or tolerates without limit; the selfless person, in truth and grace, has both love and wisdom.
think: According to Luke 17:3, what do I do when the other person repents?
How have I dealt in the past with people who only say sorry but do not change?
Whom should I go to first, to help me see my present situation clearly?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for teaching me that forgiveness and truth go together. Give me wisdom to discern what true repentance is, and courage to speak the truth when it is needed. Protect me, so that I no longer use patience to make excuses for what others do to hurt me. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, find a trusted friend or pastor and say, in three sentences, the thing that torments you most, and ask them to help you see it clearly. If you have any concern for your personal safety, please call 110 or the 113 protection hotline.
lessons.quick: Keep a heart of forgiveness ready; rebuilding the relationship depends on the other person’s real turning.
text: Be careful. If your brother sins against you, rebuke him. If he repents, forgive him.
If he sins against you seven times in the day, and seven times returns, saying, ‘I repent,’ you shall forgive him.”

lessons.title: Confess to One Another and Pray for One Another
lessons.hear:
Cheng had a secret he carried. While dating, he had once ignored and mocked his ex-girlfriend. Now he regretted it deeply, but no one knew. He had prayed about it alone several times, and still his heart felt heavy.

James says, “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed.” (Jas 5:16) So confession is not only said to God; it is also spoken out loud in front of someone trustworthy. Once it is spoken, sin loses its power to hide in the dark.

Confession is not self-flogging, and it is not asking someone else to decide what I should do. It is honesty, taking responsibility, and being loved. A partner listens without judging and simply prays with you.

Choose the right person: someone wise, who keeps confidences and does not shame others. As for whether to apologize to the person who was affected, talk it over with your partner first, to make sure it won’t hurt them again.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he sat with sinners, yet never said sin did not matter. The Bible is my standard: confess to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes me willing to bring my secrets into the light. The self-centered person hides in the dark and protects himself with face; the selfless person stands in the light and is healed by love.
think: According to James 5:16, what is the result of confessing and praying for one another?
Is there something I have kept hidden in the dark and told no one?
Which trustworthy partner can I ask to listen as I say it out loud?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for not despising my weakness. I am willing to bring what is hidden in the dark into the light. Give me courage, and prepare a wise, trustworthy partner who will listen to me and pray for me, so that I may be healed. Amen.
lessons.do: Choose a trustworthy partner and set a time, and say to them: “There is something I would like you to listen to, and to pray for me.” Send the invitation today.
lessons.quick: Once it is spoken, sin loses its power to hide in the dark.
text: Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.

lessons.title: No Excuses; Take Responsibility
lessons.hear:
Look back over this week: as the Lord forgave you, so you also forgive (Col 3:13); forgiveness is a process (Matt 6:14); rebuilding a relationship is discussed after repentance (Luke 17:3); confess to one another in the light (Jas 5:16).

Jesus told a parable: the tax collector stood far away, would not even lift his eyes to heaven, and only said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13) He did not explain, did not make excuses, and did not compare himself with others; he simply took responsibility. Jesus said this man went down to his house justified rather than the one who exalted himself.

When someone apologizes by saying, “I’m sorry, but you also…” that is not an apology; it is a defense. A true apology says clearly what I did, acknowledges the hurt it caused, and is willing to change.

This week, ask yourself: where did I see my self-centeredness? How did God support me in it?
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, and he bore my sin for me; the Bible is my standard, and the tax collector’s prayer was accepted; the Holy Spirit is my guide, leading me to face myself honestly. The self-centered person makes excuses and drags others down; the selfless person says, “It was me, and I take responsibility.” Humility overcomes pride, and all glory to God.
think: What three things did the tax collector in Luke 18:13 do?
Where did I see my self-centeredness this week? How did God support me in it?
To whom do I owe an apology with no “but” in it?
lessons.speak: Father, be merciful to me, a sinner. I no longer want to make excuses or blame others. Give me humility, so that I take responsibility honestly and have strength to repair what needs repairing. All glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, write an apology with no “but” in it: what I did; the hurt it caused you; how I am willing to change. If the person is not safe, write it down first and do not send it.
lessons.quick: A true apology has no “but,” only responsibility.
text: But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his chest, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”

weeks.keyText: bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.

weeks.title: Rebuilding Trust
weeks.theme: True repentance bears fruit; trust grows back through time and action.
group: Read 2 Corinthians 7:10. What is the difference between godly sorrow and the sorrow of the world?
What actions do you think can show that a person has truly repented?
For what matter are you willing to take an honest step this week, or ask a partner to pray for you?
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, share with a partner: “One fruit of repentance I have learned is…” and then pray for each other. Send one sentence to a friend: Tears are not repentance; fruit is.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, with a trustworthy partner, make a list of the “fruits of repentance”: no hiding, no repeating, willingness to be held accountable. Each of you picks one, and agree to ask each other about it next week. A person who has been hurt does not need to attend any occasion with the one who hurt them; if there are safety concerns, please go to a pastor or call the 113 protection hotline.

lessons.title: Godly Sorrow
lessons.hear:
Hao’s girlfriend found out he had lied. He cried and said he was sorry again and again. Three days later, though, he asked a friend, “Why hasn’t she texted me back?” He was sad because he had been found out and was afraid of losing her.

Paul distinguishes two kinds of sorrow: “For godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation, which brings no regret.” (2 Cor 7:10) The other kind is the sorrow of the world, which grieves only over one’s own loss and face, and does not bring change.

The person with godly sorrow sees this: I have hurt a person, and I have sinned against God. He is not in a hurry to be forgiven, but is willing to bear the consequences.

If you are the one who was hurt, this can help you discern: tears are not repentance, and “I’m sorry” is not change. If you are the one who did wrong, you can ask yourself: why am I sad? Is it for her, or for me?
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his sorrow was for people’s sin and suffering, not for his own face. The Bible is my standard: godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation, which brings no regret. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives people a true conviction of sin. The self-centered person grieves over loss and wants to get through it quickly; the selfless person grieves over sin and is willing to pay the price.
think: According to 2 Corinthians 7:10, what does godly sorrow produce?
Have my past apologies been more for my own sake, or for the other person’s?
How can I discern my own or the other person’s repentance today?
lessons.speak: Lord, shine your light on me, so that I can tell whether my sadness is for my face or for my sin. Give me the sorrow that is according to your will, so that I truly repent, no longer use tears to escape the consequences, and am willing to take responsibility for what I have done. Amen.
lessons.do: Take a sheet of paper and write: What am I sad about? Divide it into two columns: for myself; for the other person and for God. Then honestly pray over the second column.
lessons.quick: Tears are not repentance, and “I’m sorry” is not change.
text: For godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation, which brings no regret. But the sorrow of the world produces death.

lessons.title: Produce Fruit Worthy of Repentance
lessons.hear:
John the Baptist said to those who came to be baptized, “Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance!” (Matt 3:8) His meaning is clear: repentance must bear fruit, not just words.

Trust is like a tree that has been cut down; it takes time to grow again. It depends not on a single promise but on a series of visible actions: words and actions that match, not repeating the same harm, willingness to be transparent, not demanding that the other person forgive quickly, and being willing to accept reminders and accountability from others.

For the one who was hurt, going slowly is allowed; you do not need to rush your progress just to seem loving. You can say, “I forgive you, but I need to see time and change before I can trust again.” This is not a lack of love; it is wisdom.

For the one who did wrong, accountability is grace, not shame; it lets your change be seen, and lets someone walk with you.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he values true repentance, and he values fruit. The Bible is my standard: produce fruit worthy of repentance. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he produces the fruit of love, joy, and peace in us. The self-centered person demands that the other believe him right away; the selfless person lets trust grow back naturally through time and action.
think: According to Matthew 3:8, what must true repentance show as proof?
Do I want the other person to trust me quickly, or am I willing to prove myself through time and action?
If I am the one who was hurt, what three things would I need to see before I could trust again?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for being a God of both compassion and justice. Let my repentance bear fruit, and keep me from hurrying others to trust me. Protect those who have been hurt, and give them time, boundaries, and companions. Amen.
lessons.do: Write down three “fruits of repentance,” for example: no hiding, replying on time, accepting a partner’s questions. Pick one and start today. If you are the one who was hurt, write down the three things you need to see.
lessons.quick: Trust grows back through time and action, not through one promise.
text: Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance!

lessons.title: Zacchaeus Repents
lessons.hear:
Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector who had built his wealth by extortion, and everyone despised him. But Jesus came to his house. Moved by this acceptance, he stood up and said, “If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.” (Luke 19:8)

Notice the features of his repentance: it was proactive, not waiting for people to come and demand payment; specific, naming an amount and a proportion; and costly, giving up what had been his own. He did not demand that the people he had wronged forgive him at once, and he did not defend himself.

Jesus said, “Today, salvation has come to this house.” (Luke 19:9) God’s acceptance gave Zacchaeus the courage to face himself, and his actions afterward proved that his repentance was real.

If you have hurt someone, repentance is not just saying you are sorry, but asking: what do I need to make right? What do I need to change? And letting trusted people watch with you as you walk this road.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he accepts sinners, and he makes people willing to change. The Bible is my standard: Zacchaeus’s repentance had restitution and action. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he lets people stop protecting themselves and be willing to take responsibility. The self-centered person wants to be forgiven without paying a price; the selfless person is willing to pay the price and repair the harm.
think: What concrete actions did Zacchaeus’s repentance include?
For the person I have hurt, what do I need to make right?
To whom can I go first, and what can I do, to take an honest first step?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for coming into Zacchaeus’s house, and into my life. Make me like Zacchaeus, not afraid to face things and not afraid to pay the price. Lead me to repair what I have harmed, in a way that is safe and fitting. Amen.
lessons.do: Think of one time you hurt someone, and write down what you can do to make it right: return something, tell the truth, stop a certain behavior. Pick one to do today, or ask a partner to help you judge how to do it safely.
lessons.quick: True repentance is willing to pay the price and repair the harm.
text: Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.”
Jesus said to him, “Today, salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham.

lessons.title: A Righteous Man Falls Seven Times and Rises Again
lessons.hear:
After the breakup, Xiaoqi blamed herself: “I made the same mistake again. God must be so disappointed.” She no longer dared to pray, feeling she had no right to get up again.

Proverbs says, “a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again.” (Prov 24:16) The righteous man here is not someone who never falls, but someone who falls and gets up again. And he gets up not by his own strength, but by God’s.

After a fall, there are two directions: one is to lie still and use self-blame to prove how bad you are; the other is to admit it, repent, and let God and your partners help you up again.

Also, this verse is not an excuse for repeating harm. If the same harm keeps happening, rising up includes accepting accountability, seeking help, and changing habits. And if you are the one who was hurt, you can rise up too, slowly, with no need to hurry; God and your partners are beside you.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he lifted up Peter, and he lifts up everyone who falls. The Bible is my standard: a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he supports me to stand up again. After a fall, the self-centered person either runs away or blames himself; the selfless person brings repentance and rises again, leaning on God.
think: According to Proverbs 24:16, what does the righteous man do after he falls?
After I fall, do I often lie there blaming myself, or do I get up with repentance?
Whom can I ask for help today, so I do not face it alone?
lessons.speak: Lord, sometimes when I fall I feel I have no right to get up again. Support me, so that I repent and believe your grace is enough. Help me, after I fall, not to hide and not to blame myself, but to stand up again by leaning on you. Amen.
lessons.do: Do two things today: first, say one honest word of repentance to God; second, take one small action, such as tidying your room or sending a caring message, to show that you are getting up.
lessons.quick: A fall is not the end; rising again with repentance is.
text: for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again, but the wicked are overthrown by calamity.

lessons.title: Good News for Those Who Mourn
lessons.hear:
Look back over this week: godly sorrow (2 Cor 7:10); produce fruit worthy of repentance (Matt 3:8); Zacchaeus was willing to pay the price (Luke 19:8); a righteous man falls and still rises (Prov 24:16).

Isaiah prophesies what the Messiah will do: “to give to them a garland for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness.” (Isa 61:3) God not only forgives those who sin, he also heals those who are hurt. Ashes are exchanged for a garland, and mourning for the oil of joy.

Whether you are the one who was hurt or the one who hurt others, God has a road for you: to be healed, to be renewed, to become trees of righteousness, to the glory of God.

This week, ask yourself: where did I see my self-centeredness? How did God support me in it?
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, and he came to heal the brokenhearted; the Bible is my standard, and God turns mourning into joy; the Holy Spirit is my guide, leading us into renewal. The self-centered person is stuck in ashes; the selfless person receives the garland. Let Jesus be King, and all glory to him.
think: According to Isaiah 61:3, what does God promise to give in place of ashes, mourning, and a spirit of heaviness?
Where did I see my self-centeredness this week? How did God support me in it?
Where do I still need God’s healing? Whom can I ask to walk with me?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for coming to heal the brokenhearted. Give me a garland for my ashes, and the oil of joy for my mourning. Make me one who is renewed by you, healed in your love, giving all glory to you forever. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, write one sentence to your hurting self: “I am seen by God, and healed by God.” Then write one sentence to the person with whom you want to repair the relationship. If you need professional help, please contact a counseling organization or call the 1980 Teacher Chang counseling line.
lessons.quick: God gives a garland for ashes, and joy for mourning.
text: to provide for those who mourn in Zion, to give to them a garland for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness, that they may be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that he may be glorified.
