weeks.title: Family of Origin
weeks.theme: Home is where we learn love, and it may also hold wounds; in Christ, the past no longer decides who you are.
group: Read Psalm 27:10. How does God treat us when people abandon us?
What patterns of love did you learn in your family of origin? Which one do you want to change?
For which old pattern are you willing to take a new step this week? Ask your group to pray for you.
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, share with a partner: “One pattern passed down in my family that I want to change is…” and then pray for each other. You do not need to share details. Send one sentence to a friend: In Christ, you are a new creation.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, with a trustworthy partner, write down “three good things my family taught me” and “one thing I want to be different,” and share them. You do not need to talk about any details that make you uncomfortable. If there is any concern about abuse or personal safety, please contact a counseling organization or call the 113 protection hotline.

lessons.title: When My Father and Mother Forsake Me
lessons.hear:
When Fen was five, her father left home and rarely came back. As she grew up, she was always afraid of being left behind in dating. If the other person was even a little cold, she fell apart and looked for all kinds of ways to confirm she had not been abandoned.

David writes, “When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.” (Ps 27:10) He is not saying that parents will always forsake their children. He is telling us that even when the people closest to us hurt us, God never leaves us or forsakes us.

Our family of origin is the first place we learn love, and it holds blessings as well as wounds. Seeing these influences is not meant to blame our parents, but to keep the past from continuing to rule me in today’s relationships.

Your worth is not decided by how your parents treated you, but by how God sees you. He takes you in.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he is the Father’s beloved Son, and his identity was not decided by people’s acceptance. The Bible is my standard: when my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will take me up. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he lets me receive adoption as a child in God. The self-centered person fills the emptiness with relationships and holds on tightly; the selfless person is first taken in by God, and so has strength to love others.
think: According to Psalm 27:10, who takes me in when my parents forsake me?
Which experience from my family of origin still affects me in dating today?
How can I quietly receive “God takes me in” today?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for taking me in. My home has had gaps, and it has had wounds. Fill me with your love, so that I no longer use relationships to prove I am worth loving. Holy Spirit, heal me, so that in your arms I learn to love and to be loved. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, spend five minutes writing in your journal: one thing about love that I learned from home (good or bad). Then write after it: God says, “I will take you in.” Read it aloud once.
lessons.quick: My worth is decided by how God sees me, not by who left me.
text: When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.

lessons.title: Iniquity to the Third and Fourth Generation
lessons.hear:
Some people read the words “visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, on the third and on the fourth generation” and feel a chill: am I destined to repeat my parents’ marriage?

Let us look closely. This passage says, “visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, on the third and on the fourth generation of those who hate me.” (Exod 20:5) It describes how the consequences and patterns of sin are passed down in a family, like a river flowing from upstream to downstream. How we argue, how we handle anger, and our attitude toward conflict can all be learned by children.

But this is not a pronouncement of fate. The very next verse speaks of God showing loving kindness to those who love him. When we see a pattern, we can break it.

You do not have to prove your parents wrong, and you do not have to live in their shadow. You can choose, in Christ, to begin a new pattern, and let loving kindness be what you pass on.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he came into the world through a human genealogy, yet lived a completely different life. The Bible is my standard: the consequences of sin are passed down, and God’s loving kindness is passed down too. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he helps me see, and helps me change. The self-centered person says, “This is just how I am; I can’t change”; the selfless person says, “In Christ, I can be different.”
think: According to Exodus 20:5, how are the consequences of sin passed down in a family?
Which of my parents’ patterns do I repeat in my relationships?
Which pattern am I willing to break with the Holy Spirit’s help?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for being a God of both justice and loving kindness. Let me see the patterns passed down in my family, and keep me from using “this is just how I am” as an excuse. Holy Spirit, help me begin a new way in Christ, and let your loving kindness reach the generations after me. Amen.
lessons.do: Write down one family pattern you want to break (for example, the silent treatment, shouting, or people-pleasing), and then write down one new way of responding. The next time a related situation comes up today, try the new way once.
lessons.quick: Patterns are passed down, but in Christ they can be broken.
text: you shall not bow yourself down to them, nor serve them, for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, on the third and on the fourth generation of those who hate me,
and showing loving kindness to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.

lessons.title: The Soul Who Sins Shall Die
lessons.hear:
Jie’s father was an alcoholic who hit people. Jie resolved not to be like his father, but whenever he got angry, he felt that shadow inside himself, and he was afraid: will I become like that too?

Ezekiel says, “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son.” (Ezek 18:20) This draws a clear line for us: each person is responsible for his own choices. You do not have to bear your parents’ sins, and you cannot push your own sins onto your parents.

This brings two freedoms: first, your parents’ failures cannot condemn you; second, you can no longer say, “Because of my family, I can hurt others.”

Your past is your story, not your sentence. From today on, you can make your own choices, and you can ask a partner and God’s word to walk with you.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he bore the sin of each of us, so that we are no longer condemned by the past. The Bible is my standard: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he frees me from shame and self-blame. The self-centered person pushes responsibility onto his family or onto himself; the selfless person acknowledges the past and takes responsibility for the present.
think: According to Ezekiel 18:20, what is each person responsible for?
Do I push certain behaviors onto “that’s just how my family is”?
Have I been carrying responsibility or shame for my parents that does not belong to me?
lessons.speak: God, thank you for freeing me from the condemnation of the past. Help me no longer carry my parents’ shame, and no longer use my family as an excuse. Give me strength to take responsibility for my own choices, and to walk a new road in your grace. Amen.
lessons.do: On a sheet of paper, draw two columns: “What is someone else’s responsibility” and “What is my responsibility.” Honestly sort what comes to mind into each, and then ask God for strength for the second column.
lessons.quick: Your past is your story, not your sentence.
text: The soul who sins, he shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son. The righteousness of the righteous shall be on him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be on him.

lessons.title: Honor Your Father and Mother
lessons.hear:
Xiaoyu’s mother often used emotional blackmail: “If you loved me, you wouldn’t date.” Every time she said something like this, Xiaoyu felt unfilial and had to cancel his date.

Paul quotes the commandment: “Honor your father and mother,” which is the first commandment with a promise: “that it may be well with you, and you may live long on the earth.” (Eph 6:2–3) The original word for honor carries the sense of valuing and esteeming: respect, thanks, care, and looking after them. But honoring is not the same as obeying every demand, and it does not mean giving up your own boundaries. Grown children are to leave their parents and build their own lives (Gen 2:24).

If your parents’ words or actions make you feel controlled, shamed, or unsafe, honoring can look like this: keeping your distance, saying no in a respectful way, and continuing to pray for them. Honoring does not ask you to stay in the hurt.

If you have any concern for your personal safety, please seek help and call the 113 protection hotline.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he honored his mother and even arranged for her care from the cross, but he also obeyed the Father’s will and did not change his mission for his mother’s expectations. The Bible is my standard: honor your father and mother. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives me wisdom to find the balance between honoring and boundaries. The self-centered person trades obedience for acceptance; the selfless person respects his parents and is also loyal to God.
think: According to Ephesians 6:2–3, how are we to treat our parents?
Have I ever confused “filial piety” with “doing what I’m told”?
In what way can I respect my parents and also protect my own boundaries?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for giving me my parents. Whatever kind of people they are, I am willing to respect them. Give me wisdom to find, between honoring and boundaries, the path that pleases you. Protect me, so that I am neither controlled nor bound by resentment. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, pray for your parents for two minutes, and then write one respectful and clear sentence, for example: “I am very grateful to you, and I want to decide this myself.” Look for a chance to practice it. If there is any safety concern, please ask someone you trust for help.
lessons.quick: Honoring is respect and thanks, not giving up boundaries, and certainly not staying in the hurt.
text: “Honor your father and mother,” which is the first commandment with a promise:
“that it may be well with you, and you may live long on the earth.”

lessons.title: If Anyone Is in Christ, He Is a New Creation
lessons.hear:
Look back over this week: God takes me in (Ps 27:10); patterns can be broken (Exod 20:5); each person is responsible for himself (Ezek 18:20); honoring is not giving up boundaries (Eph 6:2).

Paul declares, “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Cor 5:17)

Being a new creation does not mean the past did not happen; it means the past no longer decides who you are. Your name is no longer “the abandoned one,” “not good enough,” or “the one from a troubled family,” but “the one in Christ.”

This is a move from the life of the old self, with its self-centeredness, into the life of the new self, with its selflessness: no longer defined by the story of my family, but led by the story of Christ.

This week, ask yourself: where did I see my self-centeredness? How did God support me in it?
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, and he gives us a new identity; the Bible is my standard, and the old has passed away and all things have become new; the Holy Spirit is my guide, and he makes the new life come alive. The self-centered person lives in the old story; the selfless person lives the new life in Christ. Let Jesus be King, and all glory to God.
think: According to 2 Corinthians 5:17, what is different about the person in Christ?
Where did I see my self-centeredness this week? How did God support me in it?
From which old label do I want to step out, and put on the name God has given me?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for making me a new creation. Keep me from being defined by the past or living in the old story. Holy Spirit, let me live out the new life, so that my family and my relationships are renewed because of you. All glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: Write down an old label and a new name, for example: abandoned → taken in by God. Put the new name next to your mirror, and read it aloud three times today. When you need to, contact a counseling organization or the 1980 Teacher Chang counseling line.
lessons.quick: The past no longer decides who you are; Christ does.
text: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.

weeks.keyText: When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.

weeks.title: Past Wounds and an Ex
weeks.theme: God can heal a wound; letting go of the past makes room for God to do something new.
group: Read Ps 147:3. How does God treat the brokenhearted?
In your past relationships, which wound still needs to be brought to God?
What boundary can you set this week to protect yourself? Ask your group members to pray for you.
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, share with a companion: “What I need God to heal right now is…,” and then pray for each other. You don’t need to share details. Send one sentence to a friend: The LORD is near to the brokenhearted.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, do one simple, restful thing with a companion: take a walk, share a meal, or exercise. You don’t need to talk about your ex or about anything that is weighing on you. When you finish, pray for each other. If you need professional help, please contact a counseling organization, the 1925 Peace of Mind Hotline, or the 1980 Teacher Chang Hotline.

lessons.title: He Heals the Brokenhearted
lessons.hear:
Kai broke up with his girlfriend of three years. His friends told him, “Pull yourself together. Stop thinking about it.” But the more he pushed his feelings down, the more he tossed and turned at night, and he lost his focus at work.

The psalmist says, “He heals the broken in heart, and binds up their wounds.” (Ps 147:3) Look at the two verbs: heals and binds up. God doesn’t tell the brokenhearted to be well right away. Like a doctor, he treats the wound layer by layer and then bandages it with care.

The pain of a broken relationship is real. It can include sadness, anger, shame, and longing, and none of these is evidence of unbelief. Bringing your tears to God is the beginning of healing.

Healing takes time, and it takes companions. You can tell God, “I’m in pain.” He won’t think you’re too fragile. He is, after all, the God who heals the brokenhearted, and he is willing to use your companions as his hands.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he wept for Lazarus and wept with those who mourned. The Bible is my standard: he heals the broken in heart and binds up their wounds. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he is the Comforter who stays with us through our pain. People who live for self suppress their emotions and want to get better fast; people who live in selflessness bring their pain to God and let him heal them.
think: What does Ps 147:3 say God does for the brokenhearted?
Have I used “pull yourself together” or “stop thinking about it” to push down what I really feel?
What can I do today to honestly tell God the pain in my heart?
lessons.speak: Lord, I am in pain, and I don’t want to pretend I’m fine. Thank you for being the God who heals the brokenhearted. Please heal me layer by layer, bind up my wounds with care, and prepare people who are willing to walk with me, so that I no longer carry this alone. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, find ten quiet minutes and write a few lines “to God”: What hurts the most right now is… Don’t edit what you write. Read it aloud to God, and then sit quietly for one minute.
lessons.quick: You can bring your heartbreak to God; he heals and he binds up.
text: He heals the broken in heart, and binds up their wounds.

lessons.title: Do Not Remember the Former Things
lessons.hear:
After her breakup, Xiaoling opened her ex-boyfriend’s social media page every day to see what he was doing and who he was with. The more she looked, the more it hurt, yet she couldn’t stop.

God said to his exiled people, “Don’t remember the former things, and don’t consider the things of old.” (Isa 43:18) Then he said, “Behold, I will do a new thing.” (Isa 43:19) This doesn’t mean pretending the past never happened, and it doesn’t forbid grief. It means we shouldn’t let the past take over what we see now, because God is about to open a new road.

To let go, you need boundaries: stop looking at the other person’s updates for a while, stop replaying conversations that hurt, and stop feeding your hope with “he’s still thinking of me.”

A boundary is not a punishment for the other person. It protects you, makes room for God to do something new, and gives you a chance to breathe again.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he set his face toward Jerusalem and was not turned aside by past rejection. The Bible is my standard: do not remember the former things; I will do a new thing. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he turns my eyes toward new places. People who live for self cling to the past and hope it will be reversed; people who live in selflessness hand the past to God and wait for his new thing.
think: What does Isa 43:19 say God will do?
Do I have a habit right now that keeps pulling me back to the past?
What boundary can I set to protect myself?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you that you will do a new thing. Help me stop looking back again and again at the wounds of the past. Give me the strength to set boundaries and to stop tormenting myself by replaying the pain. Turn my eyes toward you, and help me wait for the path you have prepared. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, do one small thing to set a boundary: hide the other person’s updates for now, delete a conversation you keep going back to reread, or put old photos away in a folder. When you’re done, pray for yourself.
lessons.quick: A boundary isn’t a punishment for the other person; it makes room for God to do something new.
text: “Don’t remember the former things, and don’t consider the things of old.
Behold, I will do a new thing. It springs out now. Don’t you know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.

lessons.title: Forgetting What Is Behind, Pressing On
lessons.hear:
Yong felt he had made too many mistakes in the past. In one relationship he had hurt someone and had also been hurt. “It feels like I’m always living in regret,” he said.

Paul had a past too: he once persecuted the church. Yet he said, “forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal.” (Phil 3:13–14) “Forgetting” here doesn’t mean losing your memory. It means no longer letting the successes and failures of the past steer my direction. Paul acknowledged his sin, received forgiveness, and then started moving forward.

To move forward, do three things first: admit what needs to be admitted, receive God’s forgiveness, and fix your eyes on Jesus.

This goal is not your next partner or a successful romance. It is Christ himself and the life he wants to complete in you. You don’t have to run alone; God and your companions are right beside you.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: for the joy set before him he endured the cross, with his eyes on what the Father had prepared. The Bible is my standard: forgetting what is behind and stretching forward to what is ahead, I press on toward the goal. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he lines my steps up with Christ. People who live for self are tied down by the shame or the glory of the past; people who live in selflessness are drawn by Christ and run straight ahead.
think: What does Phil 3:13–14 say about how Paul faced what was behind and what was ahead?
Right now, am I being held back by shame over the past, or drawn forward by Christ?
Is my “goal” Christ, or is it a certain person or a certain outcome?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for forgiving my past. Keep me from being bound by shame, and keep me from boasting in past successes. Holy Spirit, fix my eyes on Jesus, and help me walk step by step in the direction he has called me. Amen.
lessons.do: Write down three sentences: one thing I need to admit; one thing for which I will receive God’s forgiveness; and one small step I will take forward today. Keep the paper in your Bible.
lessons.quick: Forgetting what is behind doesn’t mean losing your memory; it means no longer letting the past steer me.
text: Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before,
I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.

lessons.title: The LORD Is Near to the Brokenhearted
lessons.hear:
At two in the morning, Xiaoqing couldn’t sleep again, her mind full of images from the day of the breakup. She wanted to call her ex, but she knew that would only hurt more. She opened her Bible and read, “The LORD is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.” (Ps 34:18)

God is near; he is not standing far off. In the most painful night, he is right beside you. When you can’t find words, he understands even your breathing.

There are three practical ways to be accompanied: first, speak honestly to God; second, let your body rest and keep up basic eating and sleeping; third, don’t try to carry it alone, and find someone who can walk with you.

If you find that you are down for a long time, you can’t function in daily life, or you have thoughts of hurting yourself, please tell someone near you right away, or contact professional help: the 1925 Peace of Mind Hotline, the 1980 Teacher Chang Hotline, or in an emergency, call 119.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he grieved in Gethsemane and sought both companions and the Father. The Bible is my standard: the LORD is near to the brokenhearted. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he is the Comforter who is with me forever. People who live for self grit their teeth and bear pain alone; people who live in selflessness bring their pain to God and to trustworthy companions.
think: What does Ps 34:18 say about where the LORD stands with the brokenhearted?
When I’m hurting, do I usually hold on alone, or do I find someone to walk with me?
Whom can I call or text right now?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for being near to the brokenhearted. In the darkest night, let me know that you are with me. Give me peace and rest, and prepare trustworthy companions for me, so that I no longer hold on alone, and so that when the morning comes, I am strengthened again. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, send a message to someone you trust: “I’ve been having a hard time lately. Could you keep me company and talk?” Also set aside time to rest tonight, and don’t stay up late rereading old conversations. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, contact 1925 right away.
lessons.quick: In the most painful night, God is near.
text: The LORD is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.

lessons.title: Though I Fall, I Will Arise
lessons.hear:
Look back on this week: God heals the brokenhearted (Ps 147:3); make room for God to do something new (Isa 43:19); press on toward the goal (Phil 3:14); God is near to the brokenhearted (Ps 34:18).

At a time when his nation had fallen, the prophet Micah wrote, “When I fall, I will arise. When I sit in darkness, the LORD will be a light to me.” (Mic 7:8) He didn’t deny the darkness, and he didn’t pretend he hadn’t fallen. He simply declared: I will rise, because the LORD is my light.

Rising doesn’t have to mean standing up straight all at once. Maybe it’s just sitting up. Maybe it’s just opening up to a friend.

This week you have taken one small step. God saw it, he is glad for you, and he walks with you.

Ask yourself this week: Where did I see my self-centeredness? How did God hold me up in the middle of it?
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example; he went through the darkness of the cross and rose again. The Bible is my standard; the LORD is my light. The Holy Spirit is my guide; he gives me strength to rise. People who live for self get up only by their own effort, or give up; people who live in selflessness rise slowly by the light of God. Let Jesus be King, and give all the glory to God.
think: In Mic 7:8, what does the prophet declare in the darkness?
Where did I see my self-centeredness this week? How did God hold me up in the middle of it?
What is my next small “rising”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for being my light. When I fall and sit in darkness, hold me up. Give me strength to rise step by step, and in your light help me see new hope. All glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, do one small thing that means “rising”: take a ten-minute walk, tidy up one corner, or send a message to a friend. When you’re done, write in your journal: Today I rose.
lessons.quick: Rising doesn’t have to be standing up straight all at once; one small step counts.
text: Don’t rejoice against me, my enemy. When I fall, I will arise. When I sit in darkness, the LORD will be a light to me.

weeks.keyText: He heals the broken in heart, and binds up their wounds.

weeks.title: Both Families
weeks.theme: Leaving is how we grow up; honor your parents, and take responsibility for your own decisions.
group: Read Gen 2:24. Before being joined together, what does the Bible say must come first?
What expectations does your family have about your dating and your choices? How do you respond?
What is one respectful and honest thing you can say to your family this week? Ask your group members to pray for you.
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, share with a companion: “In my relationship with my family, what I need God to heal is…,” and then pray for each other. Send one sentence to a friend: Honoring is valuing, not doing everything they say.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, arrange a small time together with your family: share a meal, make a phone call, or write a card to express your thanks. If your family relationships are tense or unsafe, you can pray for them together with a companion and seek help from a pastor.

lessons.title: A Man Will Leave His Father and Mother and Join with His Wife
lessons.hear:
Xiang had been dating his girlfriend for two years, and he asked his mom about almost everything first: which shirt to buy, where to go on the weekend, whether to keep dating. His girlfriend said, “I feel like I’m dating your mom.” Xiang felt wronged; he thought he was just being a good son.

The Bible says in Genesis, “Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.” (Gen 2:24) Notice the order: first leave, then join. Leaving doesn’t mean cutting off the relationship or no longer showing respect. It means becoming an independent adult in your emotions, your decisions, and your responsibilities.

This verse is written for people moving toward marriage, but its principle matters just as much for those who are dating: if a person’s heart hasn’t grown up out of the family they came from, it is hard to build an equal relationship with someone else.

Leaving is for the sake of loving better: your parents, and the person you will walk beside.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: at about thirty he left his hometown to begin the mission the Father had given him, yet he still cared for his mother. The Bible is my standard: a man will leave his father and mother and join with his wife. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he helps me grow to maturity in relationships. People who live for self either depend on their parents or resent them; people who live in selflessness honor their parents and also take responsibility for their own lives.
think: What does Gen 2:24 say must come first, before being joined together?
Am I responsible for my own important decisions, or do I still hand them over to my parents?
What small thing can I start with to practice being an independent adult?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving me my parents. Help me to honor them and also to learn to leave, so that I become an independent, mature person. Holy Spirit, help me answer to you for my own choices, and give me the strength to build healthy relationships. Amen.
lessons.do: Write down one small thing you have always let someone else decide for you, and make that decision yourself this time. You can ask a companion to check in: “Was this your decision?”
lessons.quick: Leaving isn’t cutting off; it’s growing up.
text: Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.

lessons.title: Honor Your Father and Mother
lessons.hear:
Xiaoxin’s parents objected to the person she was dating, only because of his family background and education. Caught in the middle, she felt that if she held her ground she would be failing to honor them, and if she gave up she would be letting herself down.

The Ten Commandments say, “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which the LORD your God gives you.” (Exod 20:12) This is the first of the commandments that face toward other people, which shows the place the family holds in God’s heart.

To honor means to value. You can value your parents’ experience, listen to their worries, and be thankful for what they have given. But valuing is not the same as doing everything they say. For an adult’s marriage and dating, the final decision must be made before God and owned by the person making it.

A good approach is this: listen first, then pray, then talk it over with a trusted pastor, and then state your decision in a respectful way. Honor and honesty do not conflict.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: on the cross he still entrusted his mother to another’s care, yet he never let family ties replace the Father’s calling. The Bible is my standard: honor your father and your mother. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives me wisdom between respect and decision. People who live for self either listen only to themselves or listen only to others; people who live in selflessness listen to God first and then speak with love.
think: What does Exod 20:12 say about how we should treat our parents?
When my parents object, do I respond with opposition or with respect?
What is one respectful and honest thing I can say to my parents?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for putting the honoring of parents among your commandments. Give me a heart that respects my parents, and give me wisdom to make decisions before you that please you. Heal the misunderstandings between me and my parents, so that love can flow. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, use one respectful sentence to thank your parents, for example: “Thank you for worrying about me; I will pray and think about it seriously.” If you need to, ask a pastor to help you communicate with your parents.
lessons.quick: Honoring is valuing, not doing everything they say.
text: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which the LORD your God gives you.

lessons.title: My Son, Listen to Your Father’s Instruction
lessons.hear:
Ade was getting ready to introduce his girlfriend to his family, but his dad spoke bluntly: “Be careful. I don’t think she’s very stable.” Ade felt a wave of discomfort; he thought his dad didn’t understand her.

Proverbs says, “My son, listen to your father’s instruction, and don’t forsake your mother’s teaching.” (Prov 1:8) Here “listen” means being willing to hear, not doing whatever they say. In the process of making choices, parents may see what we can’t see, and they may also bring their own fears and biases.

So we need to discern: which words are wise warnings, and which are control that comes from fear? You can ask yourself three questions: Are they stating facts or feelings? Is it consistent with the Bible? After hearing them out, can I still keep my peace?

The best decision brings together God’s word, the counsel of companions, your parents’ wisdom, and your own prayer.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: at twelve he sat among the teachers, listening carefully and asking questions. The Bible is my standard: listen to your father’s instruction, and don’t forsake your mother’s teaching. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he helps me discern what is a wise warning. People who live for self listen only to their own voice; people who live in selflessness listen humbly and also discern before God.
think: What does Prov 1:8 say about how we should treat our parents’ teaching?
In the warnings my parents give me, which part is wisdom and which part is fear?
Whom can I ask to help me discern my parents’ words?
lessons.speak: Lord, give me a heart that is willing to listen. Help me discern which of my parents’ words are your wisdom and which come from fear. Make me humble, and give me courage to make my own decisions before you. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, ask your parents or an older believer one question: “What do you think a healthy relationship needs?” Listen all the way through without defending yourself, and write down two points.
lessons.quick: Listening to parents means hearing them out, not doing everything they say; in the end, discern before God.
text: My son, listen to your father’s instruction, and don’t forsake your mother’s teaching;
for they will be a garland to grace your head, and chains around your neck.

lessons.title: Jesus Was Subject to His Parents
lessons.hear:
Luke records that when Jesus was twelve, he stayed behind in the temple and made his parents anxious. When they found him, “he went down with them and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them.” (Luke 2:51) Jesus knew he was the Father’s Son, yet he was still subject to his parents within the family.

This verse is set in the background of the boy Jesus, a different situation from that of an adult. It shows that being subject is a way of learning humility in the family; being subject did not diminish his identity or get in the way of his mission.

As an adult, at the wedding in Cana, Jesus also said to his mother, gently but clearly: my hour has not yet come. He was both respectful and had boundaries.

There are three ways to put this into practice: stay in touch, express thanks, and, on major decisions, explain clearly what you think and what you have prayed about, so your family knows you are not fighting them but growing up.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he was humble and obedient in the family and faithful to the Father in his mission. The Bible is my standard: he went down with them, came to Nazareth, and was subject to them. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives me both humility and clarity before my family. People who live for self either resist or try to please; people who live in selflessness show respect in love and also keep boundaries.
think: What does Luke 2:51 say Jesus did after he returned to Nazareth?
In how I relate to my family, am I distant, resistant, or respectful?
How can I take more initiative to keep a loving connection with my family?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for giving us an example: humble in the family and faithful in your mission. Teach me to be both respectful and clear before my family. Heal the distance between me and my family, so that our relationships become a place where you work. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, take the initiative to contact a family member: say hello, or set a time to have a meal together. If the relationship is tense, first pray for that person for three minutes, and then decide how to reach out. If your home is not safe, protect yourself first.
lessons.quick: Learn humility in the family, and stay faithful to God in your mission.
text: And he went down with them and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them, and his mother kept all these sayings in her heart.

lessons.title: Listen to Your Father Who Gave You Life
lessons.hear:
Look back on this week: leaving is how we grow up (Gen 2:24); honoring is valuing, not doing everything they say (Exod 20:12); hear wisdom, and also discern fear (Prov 1:8); learn humility at home (Luke 2:51).

Proverbs says, “Listen to your father who gave you life, and don’t despise your mother when she is old.” (Prov 23:22) This reminds us that parents grow old, and family needs our company. Your love life is not set against your family; it brings your family along in the vision of love.

A good relationship makes a person love their family more, not pull away from them. If you are dating, think: How does this person treat my family, and how do I treat theirs?

Ask yourself this week: Where did I see my self-centeredness? How did God hold me up in the middle of it?
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example; he loved people and loved his family. The Bible is my standard; honor your father and mother. The Holy Spirit is my guide; he enables me to live out love in my family. People who live for self treat family as obstacles or tools; people who live in selflessness treat family as people God has entrusted to them. Let Jesus be King, and give all the glory to God.
think: How does Prov 23:22 remind us to treat our aging parents?
Where did I see my self-centeredness this week? How did God hold me up in the middle of it?
What is one small thing I can do for my family?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving me my family. Keep me from looking down on my parents or overlooking their needs. Help me live out love in my family, so that your name is glorified through my family forever. All glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down three things you are thankful for about your family, and send them to one of them. If you are dating, also think of one small thing that could bless the other person’s family.
lessons.quick: A good relationship makes a person love their family more, not pull away from them.
text: Listen to your father who gave you life, and don’t despise your mother when she is old.

weeks.keyText: Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.

weeks.title: Faith, Culture, and Differences
weeks.theme: Unity doesn’t mean being exactly alike; it means accepting one another with Christ as our common center.
group: Read Eph 4:3. Who gives the unity of the Spirit? How are we to keep it?
What cultural or habit differences do you have with people close to you? Which are principles, and which are preferences?
What will you do this week to accept someone who is different from you? Ask your group members to pray for you.
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, chat for ten minutes with someone from a different background: “What is your favorite hometown food or festival?” Then pray for each other. Send one sentence to a friend: Unity isn’t being exactly alike; it is having Christ at the center.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, do something the other person enjoys with a friend whose background or personality is different from yours: eat the food they love, or join one of their activities. Afterward, share with each other: What did I learn? The other person doesn’t need to hold the same faith convictions.

lessons.title: Keep the Unity of the Spirit in the Bond of Peace
lessons.hear:
Xiaoan comes from a traditional family in southern Taiwan, and her boyfriend, En, comes from a church of a different denomination. The two discovered that even the way they pray, the time of their Sunday gatherings, and their holiday customs are different. Xiaoan asked, “Are we really a good match?”

Paul writes, “being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” (Eph 4:3) Notice that unity is given by the Spirit, and we are to be eager to keep it. We don’t reach unity by making everything the same; Christ and the Spirit join together people who are different.

Paul goes on to say that there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God. Shared core truth is the foundation of unity; as for differences in lifestyle, culture, and church style, we can learn to appreciate one another.

Unity starts with selflessness: first, I let go of “my way is the right way.”
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he prayed for his disciples, asking that they would be one. The Bible is my standard: be eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he joins different people into one body through Christ. People who live for self demand that others be like them; people who live in selflessness let Christ be the common center.
think: What does Eph 4:3 say about who gives the unity of the Spirit? What are we to do?
Which of the differences between me and the other person are about core truth, and which are about habit and culture?
What can I do today to first let go of one “my way is right” thought?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for making different people one in you. Help me tell the difference between core truth and habit and culture. Holy Spirit, make me eager to keep unity, set aside my own insistence first, and let Jesus be the common center between me and others. Amen.
lessons.do: List the three biggest differences between you and someone close to you (a friend, a family member, or someone you are dating). Next to each, mark: core truth, or habit and culture? Choose one, and learn to appreciate it today.
lessons.quick: Unity isn’t being exactly alike; it is having Christ as the common center.
text: being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
There is one body and one Spirit, even as you also were called in one hope of your calling,
one Lord, one faith, one baptism,
one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in us all.

lessons.title: The Body Is One
lessons.hear:
Amei is outgoing and loves a lively crowd; her boyfriend, Zhe, is quiet and likes to be alone. She often feels he is cold, and he often feels she is too loud.

Paul uses the body as an illustration: “For as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, being many, are one body; so also is Christ.” (1 Cor 12:12) Hands and feet are different, eyes and ears are different, but all are parts of the same body.

If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? If everyone were the same, the body would be incomplete.

Differences are not a problem; they are a design. In the body of Christ, every kind of personality, background, and gift has value. Learning to appreciate the other person’s differences makes the relationship richer and more like the body of Christ.

Of course, differences also call for communication. The two of you can learn to say: this is your way, this is my way, and together we’ll find a path of peace.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he accepted different disciples and formed them into one body. The Bible is my standard: the body is one and has many members. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he distributes gifts so that each one does their part. People who live for self try to make others into their own image; people who live in selflessness appreciate God’s design in others.
think: What illustration does 1 Cor 12:12 use to explain unity and difference?
Do I often want to change the other person so that they are like me?
Which difference in the other person can I appreciate?
lessons.speak: God, thank you for making each of us different. Help me appreciate the ways others are different from me, and stop measuring others by my own standards. Help us work together in the body of Christ, so that your name is glorified. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, give one specific word of appreciation to someone whose personality is different from yours: “I appreciate your…” Then notice how they respond, and thank God for this difference.
lessons.quick: Differences are not a problem; they are God’s design.
text: For as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, being many, are one body; so also is Christ.

lessons.title: Accept One Another
lessons.hear:
Fang’s family likes to chat loudly in Taiwanese, while the family of her boyfriend, Kai, is used to being quiet. The first time she had dinner at his home, Fang felt very uncomfortable, and when she got home she said, “I don’t think they like me.”

Paul says, “Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God.” (Rom 15:7) The standard for accepting others is the way Christ accepted us: he accepted us while we were still imperfect.

Accepting doesn’t mean agreeing with everything, and it doesn’t mean giving up truth. It means saying: I am willing to come close to you, to understand you with care, and not to meet you first with criticism.

Acceptance takes action: ask, listen, try the other person’s customs, and say how you feel. And acceptance goes both ways: I accept the other person, and I am accepted by them. When we accept one another like this, the glory goes to God.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he accepted tax collectors, sinners, and Gentiles, without asking where they came from. The Bible is my standard: accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes room in my heart for people who are different from me. People who live for self criticize first and accept later; people who live in selflessness accept first and then walk alongside.
think: What does Rom 15:7 say is the standard by which we accept others?
With people who are different from me, do I often criticize first, or get curious first?
What can I do today to accept someone from a different background?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for accepting me. Help me accept others with your heart, without criticizing first and without measuring them by conditions. Help us accept one another, so that the glory goes to you and we become your witnesses. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, ask someone from a different background one curious question: “What was Lunar New Year like at your home when you were a kid?” Listen carefully without commenting, and say, “Thank you for telling me.”
lessons.quick: Acceptance means drawing near and understanding first, not criticizing first.
text: Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God.

lessons.title: Pursue Peace and Mutual Building Up
lessons.hear:
Xiaoqi is a vegetarian, but her boyfriend, Jun, loves meat; she insists on going to the early service every Sunday, but he wants to sleep in. The two often argue over these small things, and each feels disrespected.

Romans 14 is all about believers’ differing views on food and days. Paul’s conclusion is: “So then, let’s follow after things which make for peace, and things by which we may build one another up.” (Rom 14:19) The key is “follow after”: take the initiative, and put your heart into it.

Here is how to put it into practice. First, discern: is this a question of principle or of preference? Second, on matters of preference, give way to each other and find a way that is comfortable for both. Third, on matters of principle, seek wisdom together in prayer, with a trusted pastor or companion.

Pursuing peace is not suppressing yourself; it is building each other up in love, so that the differences between two people become an opportunity to grow together.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: to make peace between people, he gave himself on the cross. The Bible is my standard: follow after things that make for peace and things by which we may build one another up. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives us wisdom and patience in our differences. People who live for self must win; people who live in selflessness are willing to give way for love and also stand firm for truth.
think: What does Rom 14:19 say we are to pursue?
Is my disagreement with the other person a matter of principle or of preference?
What is one small thing I can give way on first?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for being the Prince of Peace. Keep me from quarreling over small things, and keep me from giving way carelessly on real principles. Give me wisdom and patience, so that I pursue peace and build others up, and your name is glorified. Amen.
lessons.do: With someone you often have friction with, list three “preferences” and take the initiative to give way on one today. Keep one more, and ask a companion to help you discern: is this a principle or a preference?
lessons.quick: First tell principle from preference, then pursue peace in love.
text: So then, let’s follow after things which make for peace, and things by which we may build one another up.

lessons.title: Neither Jew nor Greek
lessons.hear:
Look back on this week: the unity of the Spirit (Eph 4:3); the body is one (1 Cor 12:12); accepting one another as Christ accepted us (Rom 15:7); pursuing peace (Rom 14:19).

Paul declares, “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” (Gal 3:28) In Christ, status, social position, and gender can never be reasons for ranking one person above another; before God every person is equally loved and equally valuable.

This doesn’t mean differences disappear; it means differences no longer become walls that divide.

This week, you may have found that in your relationships you have ranked people by background, qualifications, or habits. Bring that to the cross, and in Christ see people again.

Ask yourself this week: Where did I see my self-centeredness? How did God hold me up in the middle of it?
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example; he tore down the dividing wall. The Bible is my standard; in Christ we are all one. The Holy Spirit is my guide; he enables us to accept one another. People who live for self build walls out of differences; people who live in selflessness see brothers and sisters in Christ. Let Jesus be King, and give all the glory to God.
think: What does Gal 3:28 say happens to the walls between people in Christ?
Where did I see my self-centeredness this week? How did God hold me up in the middle of it?
Is there a wall in my heart that needs to be torn down in Christ?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for tearing down the dividing wall on the cross. Keep me from ranking people by background and conditions. Holy Spirit, help me see that every person is loved by you, and make us one in you. All glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the name of someone you have drifted from because of background or differences, pray for them for three minutes, and think of one small thing that could bring you closer, such as sending a message to say hello.
lessons.quick: In Christ, differences no longer become walls that divide.
text: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.

weeks.keyText: being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
